# Saved prompts, usage and roles

## Saved prompts

Prompts you use again and again, one Markdown file each. In the chat panel press **Prompts**: click one to put it in the message box, **Save current** to keep what you typed, **×** to delete (an **Undo** bar appears; the file waits 30 days in a trash folder).

```bash
openmaestri prompt list
openmaestri prompt read "Daily review"      # the raw text, mentions untouched
openmaestri prompt use "Daily review"       # with @file:/@note: mentions expanded
openmaestri prompt save "Daily review" "Summarise @note:Plan" [--global] [--overwrite]   # Maestro
openmaestri prompt delete "Daily review"    # Maestro
openmaestri prompt undo                     # Maestro
```

- **Where:** `~/.openmaestri/workspaces/<id>/prompts/NAME.md` for one workspace, `~/.openmaestri/prompts/NAME.md` for all. A workspace prompt hides a global one with the same name. You can edit the files with any editor; the panel updates by itself.
- **Names** use letters, digits, spaces, dots, dashes and underscores (up to 60), start with a letter or digit, and never contain `..`. Prompts are at most 64 KB. Symbolic links, FIFOs and oversized files in those folders are ignored.
- Any agent can read prompts; only a Maestro can save or delete them. A saved prompt is plain text from you or an agent: treat it as data, like a note.

## Usage and cost

```bash
openmaestri usage                 # every agent (Maestro) or just yourself
openmaestri usage "Worker" --days 7 --json
openmaestri usage report --in 12000 --out 3400 [--model deepseek-flash] [--cost 0.0021]
openmaestri usage reset ["Worker"]          # Maestro
```

The node header shows tokens and cost for each terminal. **Where the numbers come from is always shown**:

| Source | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `reported` | The agent (or a wrapper script) called `usage report`. Exact. |
| `parsed` | A line such as `Tokens: 4.5k sent, 1.2k received.` appeared in the terminal. Best effort; the format of each tool is not guaranteed, so check it once against your tool. |

There is **no estimate from terminal bytes**: agent screens redraw constantly, so byte counts say nothing about tokens. A terminal with no reported or parsed numbers shows turns and active minutes only, and `usage` says `unknown` for its tokens rather than guess.

**Prices** (USD per million tokens) are built in for `deepseek-flash` and `deepseek-v4-pro`, including DeepSeek's higher peak rate (01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, Monday to Friday), copied from the vendor's price page on 2026-11-01. Prices change: override or add models in `~/.openmaestri/prices.json`:

```json
{ "my-model": { "input": 1.0, "output": 2.0, "peak": { "input": 2.0, "output": 4.0 } } }
```

That file is read as untrusted input: only numbers from 0 to 10000 are accepted, bad entries are ignored with a note in `usage`. A DeepSeek preset implies the model in `OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL` (default `deepseek-flash`); `usage report --model` overrides it. If you pass `--cost`, your figure replaces the table's. Cost is shown only when a model with a price is known. All of it is an **estimate**, not an invoice.

Totals live in `~/.openmaestri/usage.json` (90 days of daily detail), not in the workspace file. Deleting a terminal moves its totals into an archived total.

## Roles

A role is a short set of instructions ("you are the reviewer..."). Five come built in: reviewer, tester, explorer, implementer and writer. You can add your own with `role create`, or drop `NAME.md` files in `~/.openmaestri/roles/`.

```bash
openmaestri role discover                                 # where each role comes from; repository ones are marked UNTRUSTED
openmaestri role install "Reviewer" --agent "Dev"           # dry run: shows the exact change
openmaestri role install "Reviewer" --agent "Dev" --apply   # writes it (a .bak-<time> backup first)
openmaestri role uninstall "Reviewer" --agent "Dev" --apply
```

Installing puts a marked block into the instruction file the agent already reads: `AGENTS.md` (OpenCode, Codex, Goose), `CLAUDE.md` (Claude Code) or `GEMINI.md` (Gemini CLI), in that agent's folder. Re-installing replaces the same block, never duplicates it; uninstalling removes only that block. Restart the agent afterwards so it reads the file again. Aider has no standard instruction file, so it is not supported.

Safety: it is a **dry run unless you add `--apply`**; the target must be inside the workspace and must not be a symbolic link; and roles found in the repository (`.openmaestri/roles/*.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`) are **untrusted** because anyone who can commit could have written them. Installing one needs `--trust` after you have read it. Only a Maestro can install.

# openmaestri ### A spatial canvas terminal workspace for AI agents. Open source. **Put your coding agents on an infinite canvas. Wire them together. Let one Maestro orchestrate the rest, even with cheap open models like DeepSeek.** [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-f4c430?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Node.js 22+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-22%2B-339933?style=flat-square&logo=nodedotjs&logoColor=white)](https://nodejs.org) [![PRs welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-4cc38a?style=flat-square)](CONTRIBUTING.md) [Quick start](#quick-start) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [DeepSeek and open models](#deepseek-and-open-models) · [CLI](#the-openmaestri-cli) · [FAQ](#faq) · [Docs](https://baduba.github.io/openmaestri/) · [Report a bug](docs/reporting-bugs.md)
> [!NOTE] > openmaestri is an independent, community project. It is **not affiliated with, endorsed by, or derived from the code of** the commercial app *Maestri*. It is a clean-room implementation of the same idea (a canvas of agents that can talk to each other), written from observed behavior and public documentation.
## Why Running three agents in three terminals means you are the message bus: copy this, paste that, check which one finished. openmaestri makes the agents first-class neighbors instead. - **A canvas, not tabs.** Terminals, notes and web portals live on one pannable, zoomable surface. You see everything at once. - **Connections are permissions.** An agent only sees what is wired to it. Draw a cable between two agents and they can `ask` each other. - **A Maestro that orchestrates.** Mark one agent as Maestro and it can recruit teammates, split work, run them in parallel and read their results, using the same `openmaestri` CLI available in every terminal. - **Any agent, any model.** OpenCode, Aider, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Goose, or a plain shell. Presets for **DeepSeek** are built in. - **Local and private.** One Node process on `127.0.0.1`. No account, no telemetry, no cloud. Your keys live in a `0600` file on your machine. ## Quick start ### Debian / Ubuntu (`.deb`) ```bash # Node.js 22+ is required. Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12 ship older versions in apt, # so install it first from NodeSource (https://github.com/nodesource/distributions): curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash - sudo apt install -y nodejs sudo apt install ./openmaestri_*_amd64.deb openmaestri --version openmaestri serve --open ``` Without Node 22 the install stops with "held broken packages" because the package depends on `nodejs (>= 22)`. Download the `.deb` from the [latest release](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/releases/latest). ### From source ```bash git clone https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri.git cd openmaestri npm ci # compiles node-pty: needs a C++ toolchain (build-essential, python3) npm start # prints the UI URL, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:7777/?token=... ``` Open the printed URL (it carries a one-time token that is stored as a cookie). Click **+ Terminal**, pick a preset, and you are running an agent on the canvas. ## How it works ``` ┌────────────────────────── browser (canvas UI, xterm.js) ───────────────────────────┐ │ terminals · notes · portals · connections · workspaces │ └───────────────▲──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ WebSocket (token + same-origin checks), loopback only ┌───────────────┴──────────────── openmaestri daemon (Node) ───────────────────────────┐ │ store (JSON, atomic) PTYs (node-pty) + headless xterm scheduler (routines) │ │ ▲ │ └─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ Unix socket (0600) env: OPENMAESTRI_SOCKET / TERMINAL_ID ┌───────────┴────────────┐ │ agent terminal │ agents run `openmaestri ask "Alice" "..."` │ $ openmaestri list │ and the daemon routes it to the connected terminal └────────────────────────┘ ``` Every terminal is spawned with `OPENMAESTRI_SOCKET` and `OPENMAESTRI_TERMINAL_ID`, and `openmaestri` on its `PATH`. The daemon keeps a headless xterm mirror of each screen, so `check` and `ask` return what a human would see, not raw escape codes. ## First step ```bash openmaestri doctor ``` It shows what is installed, what is missing and the command that fixes it. ## DeepSeek and open models openmaestri does not call any model itself. Your agent CLI does, so any model that your agent supports works. For DeepSeek: ```bash mkdir -p ~/.openmaestri && install -m 600 /dev/null ~/.openmaestri/env cat >> ~/.openmaestri/env <<'ENV' DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=sk-... OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL=deepseek-flash ENV ``` Then pick **OpenCode (DeepSeek)**, **Aider (DeepSeek)** or **Maestro (OpenCode + DeepSeek)** in the New terminal dialog. OpenCode also needs `opencode auth login` once (or `/connect` inside it). Details and model ids: [docs/deepseek.md](docs/deepseek.md). ## One-shot agents and what is tested Besides terminals, a Maestro can hand a job to an agent CLI in its non-interactive mode and read the answer back (`openmaestri agent claude "..."`), or give one task to several agents at once and get one report (`openmaestri run "..." --agents claude,kimi,agy --floors`). Each agent works in its own git worktree if you ask, and can run inside a Docker container with `--sandbox IMAGE`. See [One-shot agents](docs/oneshot.md). The drivers were checked against the real programs, not only against stand-ins: | Agent | Checked | | --- | --- | | Claude Code, Kimi, Antigravity (`agy`) | a full answer came back end to end | | Codex, OpenCode, Goose, Aider | run for real on a clean machine: flags accepted, the tool reaches its provider, a refused call is reported as a failure. A full answer needs your own API key, which was not used | | Gemini CLI | flags match, but Google ended it for individual accounts; use `agy` | Anything else works through a custom driver in `~/.openmaestri/settings.json`. ## The `openmaestri` CLI Available inside every terminal started by openmaestri. | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `openmaestri list` | Agents, notes and portals you can reach | | `openmaestri ask "Alice" "prompt"` | Send a prompt, wait until Alice settles, print what she produced | | `openmaestri ask --batch '{"A":"…","B":"…"}'` | Ask several agents in parallel, get a JSON array | | `openmaestri ask "Alice" --raw "2\n"` | Send raw keystrokes (menus, Ctrl-C with `\x03`) | | `openmaestri check "Alice"` | Read Alice's screen without interrupting her | | `openmaestri note create/read/write/edit/delete` | Shared notes, stored as plain Markdown files | | `openmaestri notify "msg"` | Desktop notification for the human | | `openmaestri recruit "Bob" --preset "OpenCode (DeepSeek)"` | Maestro: start a teammate wired to you | | `openmaestri routine create "nightly" --command "run tests" --daily 02:00` | Maestro: scheduled prompts | | `openmaestri guide` | The instructions an agent should follow to orchestrate well | Full reference: [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md). ## Status openmaestri is **early (0.x)** but complete in its main parts: the canvas, terminals (optionally kept alive in tmux), notes, files, portals with page automation, connections, workspaces, routines, presets and roles, git-worktree floors with snapshots, hooks and landing, saved layouts (partituras), chat threads, one-shot agents, named secrets and accounts, an optional desktop window, `.deb` packaging, and more than 200 automated tests that run real PTYs, real containers and a real browser. Left out on purpose: Android, WSL, remote tunnels, and posting reviews to GitHub or GitLab. See the [roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) and [parity with the original](docs/parity.md). ## Security An app that opens shells must be careful. The web UI listens on loopback only, requires a random per-install token, and rejects foreign `Host`/`Origin` headers (DNS rebinding). The agent socket is `0600` in a `0700` directory. Portals run in sandboxed iframes. Read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) and report vulnerabilities privately. ## FAQ **Is this the same as Maestri?** No. It is a separate open implementation of a similar idea. It shares no code with it. **Does it work on macOS or Windows?** The daemon is plain Node plus node-pty, so macOS should work from source. It is tested on Linux only. Windows needs ConPTY work. Contributions welcome. **Do I need an API key?** Only for the agent you run. openmaestri itself has no account or cloud. **Why can't an agent see another agent?** Visibility follows connections. Connect them (the ⚭ button, or `openmaestri connect A B` from a Maestro). Maestros see the whole workspace. **An agent's answer is cut off or arrives too early.** `ask` waits for the terminal to be quiet for a moment. Slow models may need `--timeout 5m`, and `check` always shows the current screen. ## Documentation - [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) · [CLI reference](docs/cli.md) · [DeepSeek and open models](docs/deepseek.md) · [Starter team](docs/starter-team.md) - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) · [How to report a bug](docs/reporting-bugs.md) - Site: https://baduba.github.io/openmaestri/ ## Contributing This is a community project and help is the whole point. Start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md); issues labelled `good first issue` are picked to be approachable. Found a bug? [Open an issue](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/issues/new/choose) and run `openmaestri debug` inside the affected terminal to attach diagnostics. ## License [MIT](LICENSE)

# Changelog

All notable changes are documented here. Format: [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com), versions follow [SemVer](https://semver.org).

## [Unreleased]

### Changed
- Docs: round 17 measured a team of seven agents (Maestro and six workers, plurality of scripts): 4 of 8 right against 6 of 8 for the trio on the same data. The starter team stays at three. `selftest` ran for real once (right, 299 s, 3 cents)

## [0.25.2] - 2026-11-06

### Fixed
- `scripts/dast.sh` exited 1 even when the ZAP baseline had no failure: the summary line `FAIL-NEW: 0 ...` matched the check for a failure. Only a count above zero fails now
- `routine create`: `--count` with a word, a decimal or zero was kept as NaN and the routine never ended; `--until` with text that is not a date was kept and the routine never stopped; `--every` past a year (for example `9999999999d`) gave a next run past the last date a Date can hold. All three are refused with a clear message

### Added
- Starter team (docs/starter-team.md): three presets, Starter Maestro (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), Starter Dev (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) and Starter Auditor (gpt-oss-120b), through OpenCode and OpenRouter, on the models that passed the runs, each changeable by a variable, plus Starter Maestro (Haiku 5.5) and Starter Dev (gpt-oss-120b), the other models with a clean record. Existing installations get them once
- `openmaestri selftest [--runs N] [--traps N] [--solo] [--budget USD]`: runs the ledger challenge (scenario C, the Dev and the Auditor compared by the program) with your models and says whether the team got it right, with a spending limit; `--solo` runs the Maestro model alone as a control. The deb package now ships the harness (`test/challenge`)
- `test/challenge/run.mjs --wide N`: one Maestro and N workers who each write their own script, the program takes the biggest group of identical outputs (a team of 7 agents is `--wide 6`), to measure whether more agents buy anything
- A seeded fuzz test of the command line arguments (20,000 random argv: the parser never throws, never pollutes Object, and `build` only fails with a usage error)

## [0.25.1] - 2026-11-05

### Fixed
- The events of a workspace (asks, checks, verdicts) are written to disk when they happen and not one second later, so a crash right after a failed check does not lose it and `resume` does not say that nothing is open

### Added
- Challenge scenario C (`--scenario c --traps 1..10`): the ledger with a dial of traps, key checked against an independent `Decimal` reading; the `--diff` mode (the program compares two independent scripts, the Maestro acts on a difference); `test/challenge/vote.mjs` (majority vote over lone runs, the control with the same compute); the answer of every run is kept in the record. Results and the stop rule in docs/models.md

## [0.25.0] - 2026-11-04

### Changed

- The spending limit also covers one-shot agents: once it is reached, `agent` and `run` are refused and one-shot agents that are running are stopped. Their own dollars are still not visible
- Challenge: `--baseline` runs one agent alone on the same task (no Maestro, teammates, check or gate) and the per-model table has a "Right answer" column, so the team can be compared with the baseline on the same footing
- Challenge: `--record` keeps the cost the agents' screens show, and the per-model table has a "Median cost per pass" column (cost and quality are different things: in a public comparison of coding harnesses the cost of one pass varied 17 times)

- docs/models.md: the baseline (one agent alone, 30 runs): 29 of 30 right, against 31 of 36 for the team, in a fraction of the time and money. On this task the team does not buy a better answer. docs/validation-done.md says what is left

## [0.23.0] - 2026-11-03

### Added
- `ask --check CMD`, `--verdict`, `--retries N`, `--then "Other"`: the program judges a teammate's work instead of the (possibly weak) Maestro. `CMD` runs in the teammate's folder and container with no keys; a failure goes back to the teammate by itself, at most twice, with the log cut to its first 20 and last 40 lines; the verdict must be an exact block and fails closed. The answer starts with `[gate] PASSED` or `[gate] FAILED`. See docs/validation.md
- `agent --check CMD`: an answer whose work fails the command goes to the next driver of the fallback chain
- `report [--json]`: what was asked, checked, rejected and corrected, written by the program from what it saw
- A loop guard on `ask`: the third nearly identical message to a teammate gets a `[loop]` warning and the fifth is refused
- Agent terminals get `PAGER=cat`, `GIT_PAGER=cat`, `GIT_EDITOR=true`, `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive` unless set, so a model that runs `git commit` without `-m` fails instead of freezing the pane
- A reviewer's verdict is one line, `VERDICT: APPROVED - reason` (the older three-line block still works); a weak model can write it, and a loose "APPROVED", "NOT APPROVED", a missing reason or a placeholder is not a verdict
- When the Maestro answers the human while the last check on some teammate's work is a failure, the program appends `[openmaestri] Not verified: ...` to that chat message and lists it as `unverified` in the report
- A watchdog for the Maestro: when the human wrote and the chat has no answer and the Maestro's screen has not changed for 45 seconds, a fixed reminder is typed into its terminal, at most twice (`OPENMAESTRI_NO_NUDGE=1` turns it off). The Maestro bootstrap no longer tells it to ask the human what the goal is
- docs/models.md: which models work as Maestro, from real challenge runs
- The Maestro guide teaches the gate and says not to ask the human what the goal is when it was already given
- Orchestration challenge: `--record FILE` and `test/challenge/summary.mjs` build a table of runs per model (docs/models.md)

### Fixed
- `ask` dropped lines that looked like old ones, so a second answer that repeated `STATUS:` or a delimiter of the first arrived without them. Screens are now compared by alignment, in order
- The `ps command` test waited a fixed half second for a process to appear and failed on a loaded machine

# Code of Conduct

We want openmaestri to be a welcoming project for everyone, whatever their experience, background or identity.

## Our standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a good environment:

- Being respectful, patient and constructive, especially with newcomers
- Giving and gracefully accepting feedback on the work, not the person
- Assuming good intent and asking when something is unclear
- Focusing on what is best for the community and the project

Unacceptable behavior:

- Harassment, insults, discriminatory jokes or personal attacks
- Publishing someone's private information without permission
- Trolling, sustained disruption of discussions, or unwelcome sexual attention
- Other conduct that would reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

## Enforcement

Maintainers may edit, hide or remove comments, commits, issues and other contributions that violate this code, and may temporarily or permanently ban contributors for behavior they judge inappropriate. Report problems privately to the maintainers through a [private security advisory](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/security/advisories/new) or by contacting the repository owner on GitHub. Reports are handled confidentially.

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant](https://www.contributor-covenant.org), version 2.1.

# Contributing to openmaestri

Thank you for helping. openmaestri is a community project: bug reports, docs, tests, new agent presets and features are all welcome.

## Ground rules

1. **Clean room.** Do not copy code, assets, prompts or text from proprietary software, including the commercial *Maestri* app. Describe behavior you want in an issue and implement it yourself. Behavior and ideas are fine; their code is not.

## Set up

```bash
git clone https://github.com/<you>/openmaestri.git
cd openmaestri
npm ci                       # needs build-essential and python3 for node-pty
npm test                     # runs real PTYs; the UI test needs Chromium
npm start                    # then open the printed URL
```

The UI test looks for Chromium via `CHROME_BIN`, then the Playwright cache. Install one with `npx playwright-core install chromium`. Without it the UI test is skipped, everything else still runs.

Use a throwaway data dir while developing so you do not touch your real workspaces:

```bash
OPENMAESTRI_DATA_DIR=/tmp/om-dev OPENMAESTRI_PORT=0 npm start
```

## Workflow

1. Find or open an issue. For anything bigger than a small fix, say what you plan to do first.
2. Branch from `main`: `git switch -c feature/short-name` (or `fix/...`, `docs/...`).
3. Keep changes focused. One concern per pull request.
4. Add or update tests. CLI behavior is tested by running `openmaestri` **inside** a terminal (see `test/e2e.test.js`); agents are faked with `test/fixtures/fake-agent.sh`, so tests need no API keys.
5. Update docs (`docs/`, README) when behavior or commands change.
6. Run `scripts/check.sh` (syntax, lint and the whole test suite), then open a pull request using the template. The project does not depend on GitHub Actions for this: everything runs on your machine (see [docs/local-ci.md](docs/local-ci.md)).

- Plain modern JavaScript (ESM), no build step, no TypeScript yet. Match the surrounding code: small functions, comments that say *why*.
- Server and CLI must run on Node 22+.
- The UI uses vanilla modules. Use `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, for anything that can contain user or agent text.
- Anything that touches the network surface (HTTP, WebSocket, socket, iframes) needs a test and a note in the PR about the security impact.

## Releases (maintainers)

Bump `version` in `package.json`, update `CHANGELOG.md`, run `TAG=vX.Y.Z scripts/check.sh --release` (checks the version matches the tag, runs the tests, builds and smoke-tests the `.deb`), then tag `vX.Y.Z` and push the tag. # Security policy

openmaestri starts shells and runs AI agents, so security bugs can be serious. Thank you for reporting them responsibly.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Do not open a public issue.** Use GitHub's private reporting:
<https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/security/advisories/new>

Please include what you found, steps to reproduce, the impact you see, and your version (`openmaestri version`). You should get a first answer within a few days. We will credit you in the fix unless you prefer otherwise.

## Supported versions

Only the latest release receives fixes while the project is 0.x.

## Audit and imports

Workspace files are validated against a closed format and a refused file changes nothing; keys, agent runs, imports and exports are written to a hash-chained audit log (`openmaestri audit --verify`). It is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof; see docs/audit.md.

## Agents, containers and hooks

One-shot agents can run in a Docker container with only the working folder shared (`--sandbox`), floor hooks can run there too, and every key travels by name. Without `--sandbox` an agent or a hook runs as you and is not isolated; see docs/oneshot.md. `openmaestri doctor` checks Docker, tmux, the permissions of `accounts.json` and `secrets.json`, and the desktop window.

## What is in scope

- Anything that lets a web page, another local user, or another origin reach the UI server, the WebSocket, or the agent socket without the token
- Bypassing the connection-based visibility rules (an agent acting on something it is not connected to) or the Maestro-only checks
- Path traversal in static file serving, note files or workspace storage
- Secrets leaking into workspace files, logs or the network
- Escapes from the portal iframe sandbox

## Design notes for reviewers

- The UI server binds `127.0.0.1` only, requires a per-install token, and checks `Host` and `Origin`.
- The agent socket is `0600` in a `0700` directory. A process that can connect already runs as the same user; the in-app permission model limits what an *agent* can do to the rest of the workspace, not what a hostile local process can do.
- Agents run with your privileges. That is inherent to terminal agents; do not point openmaestri at untrusted prompts or untrusted repositories with an agent that has shell access.

## Threat model in short

| Asset | Threat | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| A shell on your machine (the UI) | A web page or another origin reaching the server | loopback bind, 192-bit token, `Host`/`Origin` allow-list, CSP, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie |
| The agent socket | Another local user | `0600` socket in a `0700` directory |
| Workspace files | Path traversal through ids | ids must be canonical UUIDs (`safeId`) |
| Your API keys | Ending up in repositories | read from `~/.openmaestri/env`, never written to workspace files; a warning is printed if the file is group or world readable |
| The human's attention | A looping agent spamming notifications | 20 notifications per minute per terminal |
| Roles | Persistent instructions planted through a repository or a symlink | dry run by default, backup, marked block, symlink and outside-workspace targets refused, repository roles need --trust, Maestro only |
| Saved prompts and prices | Path tricks in names; hostile numbers in the prices file | strict name rule, O_NOFOLLOW reads, 64 KB cap; prices file is validated as plain numbers |
| Mentions | Reading files or notes the user did not intend to share with the agent | `@file:` only inside the workspace, 32 KB, never secret-looking, symlinks refused, preview before sending, notes limited by wiring for agents |
| Chat | Script injection through agent text; leaking files through attachments; keystrokes smuggled to the Maestro | text rendered with `textContent`; attachments only from the workspace, never secret-looking files, copied to a `0600` vault; control characters stripped; rate limit; thread ACL |
| Portal and cloud | A page or an agent reaching the machine's cloud credentials or the control port | metadata and link-local addresses and openmaestri's own port are refused in the URL check and inside the browser |
| Repositories | Code in repository hooks running during floor operations | hooks off by default, opt in with OPENMAESTRI_GIT_HOOKS=1 |
| Resource use | Recruiting terminals until the machine stalls | ceiling of 40 running terminals (OPENMAESTRI_MAX_TERMINALS) |
| Portal browsers | A page or an agent reaching local files or other processes | only http/https; `file:`/`chrome:`/`devtools:` blocked in the browser; DevTools over a pipe (no TCP port); throwaway profile per portal; uploads limited to workspace folders |
| Agent-to-agent traffic | **Prompt injection**: text returned by `ask`/`check` is untrusted input for the agent that reads it | not solvable by the app; give agents least-privilege directories and review what a Maestro recruits |

Run `scripts/sast.sh` before sending a pull request that touches the network surface. Details: [docs/security-scanning.md](docs/security-scanning.md).

# Accounts

An **account** is a named set of environment variables for an agent, so the same program can run as "work" or "personal": different keys, base URLs or organisations. It builds on [secrets](secrets.html): the key itself stays in the keyring, the account only points to it.

```bash
openmaestri secrets set work-anthropic                     # type the key once (hidden)
openmaestri accounts set work ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=secret://work-anthropic ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://proxy.example
openmaestri accounts list                                  # names and variable names, never values
```

Then use it:

```bash
openmaestri recruit "Dev" --preset Claude --account work     # a terminal agent
openmaestri preset set Claude --account work                 # every agent from this preset
openmaestri agent claude "..." --account work                # a one-shot run
openmaestri run "..." --agents claude,codex --account work   # several one-shot runs
```

In the interface, the **New terminal** window shows an *Account* list as soon as one exists.

## Rules

- A variable whose name contains `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD` or `CREDENTIAL` must be a `secret://name` reference. Plain settings (a base URL, an organisation id) may be written out.
- Names that change how a program starts are refused: `PATH`, `HOME`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_*`, `PYTHON*`, `GIT_*`, `SSH_*`, `OPENMAESTRI_*` and similar. An account is an environment, and these would turn it into a way to run code.
- The account wins over `~/.openmaestri/env` for terminals, and over the driver's own key list for one-shot runs: you chose it on purpose.
- A `secret://` reference that is not stored is left out with a warning; the reference text is never passed on as if it were the key.
- `accounts` runs only in your own shell, never inside an agent terminal. `accounts.json` is private (mode 0600). Every change is in the [audit log](audit.html), with names only.

# Architecture

```
src/store.js       workspaces, nodes, connections, notes; atomic debounced JSON writes
src/terminals.js   node-pty processes + a headless xterm per terminal (screen mirror, snapshots)
src/core.js        every command (CLI and UI) and name resolution / permissions
src/routines.js    schedule parsing and the 1-second scheduler
src/ipc.js         Unix socket server, one JSON object per line
src/server.js      HTTP + WebSocket server, auth, static files, UI protocol
bin/openmaestri.js CLI (inside a terminal) and launcher (outside)
web/               the canvas UI (vanilla ES modules + xterm.js, no build step)
```

## Why a headless terminal per agent

`check` and `ask` must return what a person would see. A TUI agent redraws its screen with cursor movement, so raw output is unreadable. The daemon feeds every byte into a headless xterm and reads text from its buffer. The same buffer yields a serialized snapshot so a reloaded browser tab restores the screen and scrollback.

## `ask` semantics

1. Resolve the target among the nodes connected to the caller (a Maestro reaches all).
2. Remember the cursor line and the time.
3. Type the prompt. If the app enabled bracketed paste, multi-line text is pasted as one unit, then Enter is sent.
4. Wait until the terminal has produced output and then been quiet for 2.5 s (0.8 s for `--raw`), or until `--timeout`.
5. Return the text from the remembered line to the end.

This is a heuristic, not a protocol: agents that stream slowly or show spinners may need a longer `--timeout`, and `check` is the escape hatch.

## Security model

- The UI server binds `127.0.0.1`, requires a 192-bit token (cookie or query), and rejects any `Host` or `Origin` that is not the loopback address and port. This blocks DNS rebinding and cross-site WebSocket hijacking.
- The agent socket is `0600` inside a `0700` directory. Anything that can connect already runs as your user, so identity is the terminal id it presents, and visibility is enforced from the connection graph.
- Portals are iframes with `sandbox`; loopback pages run without `allow-same-origin`, and pages from the openmaestri origin are refused.
- API keys come from `~/.openmaestri/env`, not from workspace files.

## Wire formats

**Agent socket** (one JSON per line):
```json
{"id":1,"ctx":{"terminalId":"…"},"cmd":"ask","args":{"name":"Alice","prompt":"…"}}
{"id":1,"ok":true,"text":"…","data":{…}}
```

**UI WebSocket** messages carry a `t` field: `workspace.select`, `node.create`, `node.patch`, `conn.create`, `term.attach`, `term.in`, `term.resize`, and so on. The server pushes `workspace` (full state of the changed workspace), `term.out`, `term.snapshot`, `term.status`, `notify`.

## Tests

`npm test` runs real PTYs: the CLI is executed *inside* terminals to prove the whole path. The UI test drives headless Chromium with `playwright-core`.

# Audit log and workspace files

## The audit log

openmaestri keeps a record of the things that change your machine's state through it, in `~/.openmaestri/audit.log` (mode 0600), one JSON line per event:

| Event | When | What is stored |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `secret.set`, `secret.remove` | `openmaestri secrets ...` | the name and the backend, never the value |
| `agent.run`, `run` | a Maestro starts one-shot agents | driver names, who asked, the folder name, the size of the prompt and its SHA-256, never the prompt |
| `workspace.import` | a workspace file is loaded in the UI | accepted or refused, the first reason, node counts, how many commands were held back |
| `workspace.export` | a workspace file is downloaded | the workspace name and node count |

```bash
openmaestri audit --tail 30      # the last events
openmaestri audit --verify       # check the whole chain
```

Each line carries the hash of the line before it. `--verify` fails, and says at which line, when a line was **edited, removed, repeated, reordered** or when the end of the log was **cut off** (a small `audit.log.head` file remembers where the log should end).

What it is not: it is tamper-**evident**, not tamper-proof. A program that runs as you can rewrite `audit.log` and `audit.log.head` together. Copy the `head` line from `--verify` somewhere else now and then if you want an anchor it cannot reach. The `audit` command refuses to run inside an agent terminal.

## Workspace files (export and import)

A workspace file (`*.openmaestri.json`) has a **closed format**, version 1. On import every field is checked, and a file is refused as a whole, with the reasons listed, when it has:

- a field the format does not define (at any level), or a field of the wrong type;
- a version other than 1, a node kind that does not exist, or a connection that is not exactly `{from, to}`;
- more than 2000 nodes, a note over 1 MB, more than 20 MB of text, or nesting deeper than 12 levels.

A refused file creates nothing and is recorded in the audit log. Ids in the file are never reused, and a terminal command that arrives in a file does not run until you trust it. Exporting then importing gives back the same structure. Files nodes (folder browsers) are not part of the format; they are a view, not content.

--- title: Chat with your Maestro --- # Chat with your Maestro The chat is a conversation between you and your **Maestro**. You write in the side panel (the **Chat** button, top toolbar); the message is stored and typed into the Maestro's terminal. The Maestro answers with the `openmaestri say` command, and the answer appears in the panel. Everything else it does (recruiting teammates, asking them, writing notes) shows on the canvas as usual. ## Seven threads Each workspace has **seven fixed threads** (1 to 7), shown as tabs. Double-click a tab to rename it. The active thread is where agents write; unread counts show on the other tabs. A thread keeps its history across restarts, and clearing one never touches the others. ## What the Maestro uses | Command | Does | |---|---| | `openmaestri say "text"` | Answer in the active thread | | `openmaestri say --progress "text"` | A short status line that is shown while it works and replaced by the final answer; never stored | | `openmaestri say --file PATH` | Send a text file as the message, or an image as an attachment | | `openmaestri say --attach PATH ... "text"` | Hand over files with the answer | | `openmaestri say --thread N "text"` | Write to another thread (Maestro only) | | `openmaestri recall` | The recent messages of the active thread (`--turns N`, `--last day\|week\|month`, `--from DATE [--to DATE]`, `--json`) | | `openmaestri recall N` | Another thread (Maestro only); `--all` reads every thread (Maestro only) | | `openmaestri recall list` | The seven threads, empty ones marked | | `openmaestri recall attachment ID` | Where an attachment is stored, readable by you | `openmaestri guide` tells an agent all of this. A preset with **Maestro** ticked, for example *Maestro (OpenCode + DeepSeek)*, already starts with the right instructions. ## The panel - Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line. The square button interrupts the Maestro (Ctrl-C into its terminal). - The search box looks through all seven threads. - When the Maestro answers and waits for you, its node on the canvas glows and the Chat button shows a dot. Selecting the node, or writing again, clears it. Terminals that call `notify` glow the same way. ## Where it lives and what is protected Messages are append-only files under `~/.openmaestri/workspaces//chat/threads/` (mode `0600`), not in `workspace.json`, so a long conversation never slows the canvas. A thread file past 8 MB keeps its newest 3000 messages. - **Attachments** are copied into a vault (`chat/vault//`, content addressed, immutable). A file must be a regular file **inside the workspace or one of its floors** (symlinks are resolved first), at most 10 MB, and not look like a secret (`.env*`, `id_*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, key stores, `credentials*`, `.netrc`, `.npmrc`, anything named `*secret*`). - **Text from agents is never HTML.** The panel writes it with `textContent`; a message such as `` is shown as characters. This matters because this page can drive shells. - **Control characters** (ESC, NUL, Ctrl-C...) are stripped before a message is stored or typed into a terminal, so a message cannot send keystrokes to the Maestro. - **Limits:** 20,000 characters per message, 30 `say` per minute per terminal. - **Who can read what:** a Maestro can read every thread; any other agent can read only the active thread and cannot use `--all`. - Chat text is data written by agents and humans; treat anything an agent pastes from the web as untrusted input. ## Mentions (the prompter) Type `@` in the message box. A popup lists agents, notes and workspace files; arrows move, Enter or Tab inserts, Escape closes. A mention is a typed token you can also write by hand: ``` @agent:Alice @note:"Release plan" @file:src/app.js ``` When you send, the thread keeps your text as written, and the Maestro receives it with the mentions **expanded**: a note becomes its text, a file becomes its content, each fenced by a random boundary the content cannot forge. **Preview** shows exactly what will be sent, including anything that was left out and why. Rules for `@file:`: inside the workspace or one of its floors only (symlinks that leave it are refused), a regular text file of at most **32 KB**, never one that looks like a secret (`.env*`, keys, credentials). The picker skips `.git`, `node_modules`, build folders, binaries and secret-looking files, never follows symlinks, and stops scanning as soon as you type again. Agents can run `openmaestri prompt materialize "..."` too, but only see notes and agents wired to them. ## The Maestro must be an agent A message is typed into the Maestro's terminal. If its agent has exited, that terminal is a plain shell, and typing your message there would run it as commands, so openmaestri refuses and tells you to restart it. The same applies to a Maestro that was created without an agent command. ## Long threads and memory A thread that reaches 200 messages is condensed on its own: everything except the newest 40 messages is **appended to an archive file first** (`thread-N.archive.jsonl`, never deleted), then summarised, then removed from the active file. If the machine dies halfway, nothing is lost: at worst a message exists in both files and is shown once. The summary is built by fixed rules, **locally, with no model and no network**: who spoke and when, what the human asked, lines that read like decisions or rules ("we decided...", "never..."), questions that may still be open, files and attachments mentioned. It only quotes the thread, so it cannot contain anything that was not said, and obvious credentials (keys, tokens, `password=...`, private keys) are masked in it. The panel shows it above the messages ("Earlier messages are summarised"). Up to eight parts are kept; older parts stay in the archive. | Command | Does | |---|---| | `openmaestri recall` | Recent messages, preceded by the summary when there is one | | `recall --summary` | Only the summary | | `recall --archive` | Also the archived messages (a `--from` date that reaches back includes them too) | | `openmaestri memory status [N]` | Active, archived and summary parts per thread | | `openmaestri memory compress [N]` | Condense now (Maestro) | A summary written by a model is not offered: it would send your conversation to a provider, so it would have to be an explicit opt-in, and it is not built. ## Not implemented yet Dragging files into the panel. ## Dropping files Drag a file onto the chat panel and it goes to your Maestro with whatever you had typed as the message (up to three files at a time, 10 MB each). The Maestro is told the file's id and can get its path with `openmaestri recall attachment ID`. The file is kept in the chat's private vault, not in your project. Files that look like secrets (`.env`, private keys, names like `id_rsa`) or contain a private key are refused, and so are empty files.

# CLI reference

`openmaestri` works inside terminals started by openmaestri (it needs `OPENMAESTRI_SOCKET`). Outside a terminal, `openmaestri [serve] [--open]` starts the app. Add `--json` for machine output where supported.

An agent sees only what is connected to it. A **Maestro** terminal sees the whole workspace and can run the commands marked *(Maestro)*.

## Talking to agents

| Command | Description |

| `list` | Reachable agents, notes, portals with status |
| `ask "Agent" "prompt" [--timeout 120s]` | Type the prompt (bracketed paste for multi-line), wait until output is quiet, print the new screen text |
| `ask "Agent" "prompt" [--check CMD] [--verdict] [--retries N] [--then "Other"]` | The program judges the answer: `CMD` must exit 0 in the agent's folder, `--verdict` needs an exact verdict block. A failure goes back to the agent (at most 2 times), then to `Other`. The answer starts with `[gate] PASSED` or `[gate] FAILED`. `--check` is Maestro only. See [checking work](validation.html) |
| `budget` | What the agents' screens say was spent against the limit the person set with `OPENMAESTRI_BUDGET_USD`. Read only |
| `sandbox` | Where each teammate runs (box or this machine) and the names of the keys the ones on this machine can read. Read only |
| `resume` | What happened in this workspace before you started and what is still open. Survives restarts |
| `recruit ... --no-sandbox` | Run this teammate on this machine even when a default box is set |
| `report [--json]` | What was asked, checked, rejected and corrected in this workspace, written by the program |
| `ask --batch '{"A":"…","B":"…"}'` | Parallel asks, JSON array `[{agent,state,output}]`; `state` is `idle`, `timeout` or `exited` |
| `accounts set NAME VAR=value ... \| list \| rm NAME [VAR ...]` | (your own shell) Named environments for agents. See [accounts](accounts.html) |
| `partitura export "Name"` / `partitura import FILE [--name N]` | A layout as a file, and back (imported commands are held back) |
| `routine history "Name"` | The last 20 runs of a routine: when, scheduled or manual, ok or failed |
| `floor hooks "Floor" [--post-agent CMD] [--pre-land CMD] [--rollback-on-fail on\|off] [--clear-hooks]` | Checks after each agent and before landing. See [floors](floors.html) |

## Other

`say`, `recall` and `prompt parse|materialize` are the chat commands (see [Chat](chat.html)). `openmaestri doctor` checks the installation and prints how to fix what is missing (it works in any shell, with or without the app running). `openmaestri selftest` runs the ledger challenge with your models and says whether the team gets it right on your machine (needs OpenCode and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` for the starter team; `--runs 2` by default, a few cents, `--budget 1` dollar limit, `--solo` for the control with one agent; see [starter team](starter-team.html)). `openmaestri guide` prints the orchestration instructions for agents. `openmaestri debug` prints diagnostics (attach it to bug reports). `openmaestri version`.

## Exit codes

`0` success · `1` command failed (message on stderr) · `2` usage error or not inside an openmaestri terminal.

# DeepSeek and open models

openmaestri never talks to a model. The agent CLI inside each terminal does. So "using DeepSeek" means running an agent CLI that supports it. Two work well today.

## 0. Check your machine

```bash
openmaestri doctor
```

It tells you whether `opencode` or `aider` is installed, whether a DeepSeek key is set (never printing it), and whether the keys file is private. Fix what it flags first; a DeepSeek preset cannot work without the agent program.

## 1. Put the key where openmaestri can inject it

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.openmaestri
install -m 600 /dev/null ~/.openmaestri/env
cat >> ~/.openmaestri/env <<'ENV'
DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=sk-your-key
OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL=deepseek-flash
ENV
```

Every terminal openmaestri starts receives these variables. They are never written to `workspace.json`, so you can share or commit a workspace without leaking a key. Terminals that are already running keep their old environment, so create a new terminal after changing the file.

Create a key in the [DeepSeek console](https://platform.deepseek.com/).

## 2. OpenCode

[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) is a terminal coding agent with a DeepSeek provider.

```bash
opencode auth login      # choose DeepSeek and paste the key (stored in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json)
opencode models deepseek # lists valid model ids, in provider/model form
```

The built-in presets run `opencode -m "deepseek/${OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL:-deepseek-flash}"`. `deepseek-flash` and `deepseek-v4-pro` are the model names on DeepSeek's API price list at the time of writing. If `opencode models deepseek` shows different ids, set `OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL` in `~/.openmaestri/env` to one that it lists.

## 3. Aider

```bash
pip install aider-chat
```

The *Aider (DeepSeek)* preset runs `aider --model "deepseek/${OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL:-deepseek-flash}"` and reads `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`.

## 4. A Maestro on DeepSeek

Choose **Maestro (OpenCode + DeepSeek)** in the New terminal dialog. It starts OpenCode on DeepSeek with the Maestro flag, then sends it an opening instruction: run `openmaestri guide` and ask you for the goal. The guide teaches it to recruit teammates, share context in notes, use `ask --batch` for parallel work, and report progress.

Pick the model when you recruit: `openmaestri recruit "Deep" --preset "OpenCode (DeepSeek)" --model deepseek-v4-pro`. The model also drives the cost estimate in `openmaestri usage`. `recruit` checks that the agent is installed and says so if it is not (`--no-check` skips that).

Teammates can run on other models. A good pattern for cost: a stronger model as Maestro, DeepSeek workers.

```bash
openmaestri recruit "Backend" --preset "OpenCode (DeepSeek)" --dir ./api
openmaestri recruit "Tests"   --preset "Aider (DeepSeek)"    --dir ./api
```

## Custom presets

A preset is just a shell command. Add your own from a Maestro:

```bash
openmaestri preset create "Local Ollama" --command 'aider --model ollama_chat/qwen2.5-coder'
```

Anything that runs in a terminal can be an agent: other providers, local models through Ollama, a script.

## Tips for cheaper models

- Keep prompts concrete and short. Put shared context in a note instead of repeating it.
- Give each worker one directory and one task.
- Use `check` before assuming a worker finished; slow models need `ask --timeout 5m`.
- Keep the Maestro's guide in view: `openmaestri guide` is what it should follow.

# Desktop window

openmaestri runs in your browser. If you prefer a window of its own, there is an optional shell built on Electron: one window, a tray icon, and system notifications for the agents' messages. It shows the same page as the browser and adds no extra powers to it.

```bash
npm --prefix /usr/lib/openmaestri/app/desktop install    # once (downloads Electron, about 100 MB)
openmaestri desktop
```

From a source checkout the folder is `desktop/`. It needs Node.js 22 or newer on the `PATH` (or `OPENMAESTRI_NODE`).

- It starts `openmaestri serve` for you, or attaches to the one already running, and stops only the daemon it started when you quit.
- Closing the window hides it to the tray (when your desktop shows tray icons); *Quit* in the tray menu ends everything. Only one window can be open.
- Safety: the window is sandboxed, has no Node integration and no preload script, may only show the daemon's own address, and sends web links to your browser. Only notifications are allowed as a permission; camera, microphone and location are refused.
- Electron is not part of the `.deb` and is not installed by default; the rest of openmaestri does not depend on it.

## Preferences

*Preferences* in the command palette (Ctrl+K) shows the version, the data folder and the secret store, switches persistent terminals on or off, and brings the welcome screen back. This works in the browser too.

# Everyday tools

Small things that make a busy canvas easier to live with.

## Processes and memory

```bash
openmaestri ps                      # every terminal you can reach: process count, memory, CPU
openmaestri ps --all                # and each process below it
openmaestri ps stop "Builder" 4242  # ask one process to stop (add --force to kill it)
```

`ps` reads `/proc`, so it is for Linux. `ps stop` only works on a process that runs *below* that terminal's shell, so it cannot be aimed at anything else on the machine; to stop a whole terminal use `dismiss`.

## Workspaces: icons, groups, unload

```bash
openmaestri workspace set "Client A" --icon 🚀 --group Clients
openmaestri workspace unload "Client A"      # stop its terminals and portals, keep everything
```

Groups become collapsible headings in the sidebar, an icon sits before the name, and a dot shows when a workspace has running terminals. In the interface, open the command palette (Ctrl+K) for *Workspace: set icon and group* and *Workspace: stop everything running in ...*. Unloading frees memory without deleting anything: the terminals start again when you open the workspace.

## Notes

- **Preview** in a note's toolbar shows it as formatted Markdown.
- **Pictures:** drop or paste a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP onto a note (up to 5 MB). It is stored in the workspace's private vault and a `![name](/attachment/...)` line is inserted. Pictures are recognised by their content, not their file name, and SVG is not accepted because it can carry script.
- **A file as a note:** `openmaestri note from-file docs/plan.md` copies a text file of the project (up to 32 KB, nothing that looks like a secret) into a new note.

## Chat

- **Copy** (⧉) puts the thread on the clipboard as text, **Download** (⭳) saves it as a Markdown file. Credentials are masked in the download.
- **A summary written by an agent you choose:** `openmaestri chat summarize --with claude` sends the thread (credentials masked) to that agent as a one-shot run and keeps the answer. `recall --summary` then shows it next to the rule-based summary, labelled with who wrote it and when. Nothing is sent anywhere unless you run this.

# Files

A **Files** node (`+ Files` in the toolbar) shows the folder of the current floor, or the workspace folder on the ground floor, as a tree with a plain text editor beside it. It is for reading and fixing a file while you watch your agents work, not a replacement for your editor.

## What it does

- **Tree**: folders open on click; `.git` and `.openmaestri` are never shown. Files git reports as modified (orange), new (green) or deleted (red) are marked.
- **Editor**: `Ctrl+S` saves. A dot shows unsaved changes. Files over 1 MB and binary files are not opened.
- **Versions**: every save keeps the previous content (the last 10, under the workspace data folder). Pick one from the **Versions** list to bring it back into the editor, then save to keep it.
- **Markdown preview**: `Preview` renders headings, lists, quotes, code blocks, bold, italic, code and `http(s)` links. Raw HTML in the file is shown as text, never run.
- **New, rename, delete**: delete moves the item to a trash next to the version backups; nothing is erased outright.

## Tabs, search and colours

- **Tabs:** every file you open gets a tab. Switching keeps each file's unsaved text, and a ● marks a tab with changes.
- **Search:** the box above the tree searches the text of all files below the folder (not a pattern, case does not matter, two characters at least). It skips `node_modules`, build folders, `.git`, binaries, files over 1 MB and symbolic links, and stops at 200 matches. Click a result to open the file at that line.
- **Colours:** comments, strings, numbers and keywords are coloured for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON, Python, shell, YAML and CSS files up to 200 KB. It is colouring, not parsing, so unusual code just looks plain.

## Safety rules

- Every path is checked after resolving symbolic links, and must stay inside the folder of the node. `..`, absolute paths, backslashes and NUL are refused.
- A symbolic link that points outside the folder is not listed and cannot be read; a symbolic link is never written through.
- A save is refused when the file changed on disk after you opened it (an agent may have edited it): reload, or copy your text first.
- A save writes a temporary file and renames it, and keeps the file's permissions.
- Reads use one descriptor and never block on a pipe.

## From a script

The same operations travel over the UI WebSocket as `files.op` (`list`, `read`, `write`, `create`, `rename`, `remove`, `status`, `versions`, `version`) and are only accepted for a node of kind `files`.

# Floors

A workspace has a **ground floor** (the project directory) and any number of extra **floors**. Each floor is its own canvas. In a git project a floor can also have its own checkout and branch, so agents on different floors never edit the same files.

## Why

Three agents on three features in one working tree step on each other. Give each feature a floor: its agents run in that floor's folder, on that floor's branch. When a feature is done, **land** the floor: its branch is merged into the project and the floor goes away.

## Kinds

| Kind | What it is | When |
|---|---|---|
| `worktree` | `git worktree add` under `<project>/.openmaestri/floors/<name>`, on a new branch `floor/<name>` | default in a git project; cheap, shares objects |
| `clone` | an independent `git clone --local` (`--copy`) | full isolation (own `.git`, own hooks) |
| `dir` | a folder you already have (`--dir PATH`) | your own worktree; nothing is checked out |
| `plain` | no checkout; shares the project folder (`--no-git`, or not a git project) | notes-only or non-git work |

The floors folder is added to the repository's `.git/info/exclude`, so it never shows up in `git status`.

## From the CLI (Maestro)

```bash
openmaestri floor create "Login" [--branch B] [--existing-branch] [--copy] [--no-git] [--copy-ground] [--partitura P]
openmaestri floor create "Mine" --dir ~/work/my-worktree
openmaestri floor prs                               # open pull/merge requests with their checks
openmaestri floor create --pull-request 123          # fetches the pull request into a floor (GitLab: merge request)
openmaestri recruit "Dev" --preset "OpenCode (DeepSeek)" --floor "Login"
openmaestri floor status "tests passing" --state review --progress 4/5
openmaestri floor list
openmaestri floor land "Login" [--into main] [--delete-branch] [--keep-floor]   # from the ground floor
openmaestri floor delete "Login" [--keep-branch] [--keep-folder] [--force]       # from the ground floor
openmaestri floor unload "Login"                      # stop its terminals; they restart when you open the floor
```

Agents see the cables that reach them, as always. A Maestro also sees everything on its own floor. `recruit --floor` places the teammate on another floor and wires it to you across floors.

## From the UI

The floor bar at the bottom left switches floors (`+ Floor` creates one). The palette (Ctrl+K) has `Go to floor`, `Land floor`, `Delete floor` and `Floor status`. Each floor remembers its status message, shown in the toolbar.

## Landing, safely

`floor land` refuses unless both the floor and the ground floor have no uncommitted changes. It merges the floor's branch into the project's current branch (or `--into BRANCH`). If the merge conflicts, it **aborts the merge, changes nothing, keeps the floor**, and lists the conflicting files; merge the project branch into the floor first and resolve them there.

`floor delete` refuses a floor with uncommitted changes unless `--force`, and keeps a branch that has unmerged commits (it tells you).

## Limits

- Undo/redo covers the canvas of every floor, but creating or deleting a floor itself (and its checkout) is not undoable.
- Hooks that run on floor creation or landing are not implemented yet.
- **Repository hooks do not run** during floor operations (`post-checkout`, `pre-merge-commit`...): they are code from the repository. Set `OPENMAESTRI_GIT_HOOKS=1` before starting openmaestri if you want them.
- Everything shells out to your installed `git`, with argument arrays (no shell), validated branch names and a 60 second timeout.

## Pull requests and merge requests

`openmaestri floor prs` lists the open pull requests (GitHub, through `gh`) or merge requests (GitLab, through `glab`) of the workspace repository, with the state of their checks:

```
#12   ok   feat/x         ana     Add the files browser
#9    FAIL draft wip      bo      WIP
```

`ok`, `FAIL`, `...` (running) and `-` (no checks) come from GitHub's check results. GitLab's list does not include pipelines, so merge requests show `?`. `--json` prints the rows for scripts, `--provider github|gitlab` is needed only when the `origin` URL is on a self-hosted host.

Then `openmaestri floor create --pull-request 12` (a number, `#12`, or the page URL) fetches that request into its own floor, on a branch `pr-12`, so an agent can review or fix it without touching your checkout.

- It uses **your** `gh` or `glab`, already signed in; openmaestri never sees or keeps a token. If the program is missing, the message tells you where to get it.
- It is read-only: nothing is pushed, commented or merged. Titles, branch names and authors are written by other people, so control characters and direction-changing characters are removed before they are shown.
- A `gh` or `glab` that resolves inside the workspace is refused, like the agent CLIs.

## Snapshots and rollback

A snapshot remembers every file of a floor at one moment: edited files, new files and deletions. Ignored files (what `.gitignore` lists) are not part of it. It is stored inside the repository as a hidden git object under `refs/openmaestri/snapshots/`, so nothing appears in `git status`, `git log` or your branches.

```bash
openmaestri floor snapshot "Work" --label "tests pass"
openmaestri floor snapshots "Work"          # newest first
openmaestri floor rollback "Work"           # back to the latest one
openmaestri floor rollback "Work" 20261102093015123-a1b2
```

- **A rollback can be undone.** Before putting the files back it takes a snapshot of how they are now, and prints the command that returns to it.
- **Automatic ones.** `openmaestri run --floors` takes a snapshot of each agent's floor when the agent finishes (the report prints its id), and `floor land` takes one just before landing.
- **What it restores:** files. It does not move the branch: commits made after the snapshot stay (the rollback tells you when that happened), and the staging area is not restored.
- It refuses while an agent in that floor is printing output, because files would change under it.
- Only the last 20 snapshots of a floor are kept, and deleting the floor removes them. A snapshot of a floor with very large files takes room in `.git`.
- A tree with more than 20000 new files that git does not ignore (for example a `node_modules` that is missing from `.gitignore`) is refused with advice, because every snapshot would be slow and heavy. `OPENMAESTRI_SNAPSHOT_MAX_FILES` raises the limit.
- It needs the floor folder to be the top of a git repository or worktree. The ground floor works too.

## Ports and compose projects per floor

Worktrees separate files, not the machine. Two agents that each start a dev server on 3000, or a database on 5432, collide. So every floor has its own block of 100 ports (from 20000, never given twice across your workspaces), and everything started in it (terminals, hooks, one-shot agents) sees:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `OPENMAESTRI_PORT_BASE` | The first port of the block, for example `20100`. Use `$OPENMAESTRI_PORT_BASE + 1`, `+ 2`... for the other services |
| `PORT` | The same number, set only in real floors (many dev servers read it). Your own `PORT` in `~/.openmaestri/env` wins |
| `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` | `om-<workspace>-<floor>`, so `docker compose up` in two floors does not reuse containers and networks. Real floors only |
| `OPENMAESTRI_FLOOR` | The floor name, or `ground` |

The ground floor only gets `OPENMAESTRI_PORT_BASE`: what you already run there does not change. In a compose file use `"${OPENMAESTRI_PORT_BASE:-5432}:5432"`.

## Hooks

A hook is a check that runs on a floor at two moments. You set them per floor:

```bash
openmaestri floor hooks "Work" --post-agent "npm test" --pre-land "npm run lint" --rollback-on-fail on
openmaestri floor hooks "Work"                 # show
openmaestri floor hooks "Work" --clear-hooks
```

- **`--post-agent`** runs in the floor folder after each agent of `openmaestri run --floors` finishes without error. The result (passed, failed, timed out, and the last lines of output) is in the report. With `--rollback-on-fail on`, a failing check puts the files back to how they were before the agent started; the agent's work stays in its *after* snapshot.
- **`--pre-land`** runs before `floor land`. If it fails, nothing is landed and the output is shown. `floor land "Work" --no-hooks` skips it on purpose.
- **In a container:** `floor hooks "Work" --sandbox my-image` runs both hooks inside a Docker container (only the floor folder, at `/work`, your user id, no capabilities). A `run --floors --sandbox IMAGE` checks each agent's work in a container too, unless the floor names its own image. Without a sandbox a hook runs on this machine.
- A hook is a shell command you wrote for your project. It runs with the same rights as a terminal, but with a short environment (no API keys), no input, and a time limit of 5 minutes (`OPENMAESTRI_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS`); on timeout the command and everything it started are stopped.
- Every run is in the [audit log](audit.html), and only a Maestro can change hooks.

# Orchestration challenge (functional test)

A test of the whole product with real agents: a Maestro has to coordinate teammates through several round trips, with data that must come back, decisions that depend on it, and a reviewer that can send the work back.

## The task

The folder has `data/sales.csv` (about 250 rows, with refunds and repeated orders) and `data/rules.md` (what makes a row valid, how revenue is summed, when a region is flagged). The Maestro must not read the data or compute anything. It has to:

1. recruit an **Auditor** and have it restate the rules from the file;
2. recruit a **Dev** and hand it the rules (not the file) to write `flag.py`;
3. run `flag.py`, send the output to the Auditor for **APPROVED** or **REJECTED**;
4. on REJECTED, send the reason back to the Dev and go again (at most 5 rounds);
5. answer the human in the chat with `VERDICT`, `FLAGGED` and `ROUNDS`.

The data comes from a seed, and the answer key is computed by the harness, so the result is checked, not judged by eye. The key differs from the naive reading of the data (every row counts), which is what makes the feedback loop necessary.

## Running it

```bash
# with real agents (a Maestro terminal and a Worker preset, any command)
node test/challenge/run.mjs --maestro 'opencode -m opencode/big-pickle' --worker 'opencode -m opencode/big-pickle'

# with scripted agents (no model; this is what npm test runs)
node test/challenge/run.mjs --scripted
```

Options: `--record FILE` (append one line per run for the [per-model table](models.html)), `--inject` (see below), `--seed N`, `--timeout MIN` (default 30), `--stall MIN` (give up after this long without any terminal output, default 8), `--boot SECONDS`, `--out DIR`.

It prints one line and writes `report.md` and `result.json` (the checks, the messages delivered to each teammate with times, the final chat answer, the last lines of every terminal) and a copy of `flag.py`.

## What is checked

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| final answer says APPROVED | the loop closed |
| flagged regions equal the key | the result is right |
| `flag.py` exists and prints the key | the work product is right, not only the claim |
| Auditor and Dev were recruited | recruiting works |
| Auditor asked at least twice, Dev at least once | there were round trips |
| the Maestro did not read the data itself | it delegated |
| no message to a teammate was sent twice | the answer of `ask` reached the Maestro, so it had no reason to ask again |
| the Maestro did not dictate sales figures to a teammate | the Auditor's verdict comes from its own reading of the data, not from the Maestro's |

With `--inject` the harness also plants a bug in `flag.py` (every row counts, the classic mistake) the moment the Dev hands it over, before the Maestro runs it. Without it a capable Dev gets it right at once and the review loop is never exercised: an `APPROVED` after one round proves little. With it three more checks apply:

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| the Auditor said REJECTED | the review caught a real defect by reading the data |
| the Dev was asked again after the rejection | the feedback went back to the author |
| `flag.py` was fixed, not left as planted | the loop ended with a corrected work product |

Two more checks apply with `--inject`, on the oracle itself:

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| the Auditor's `verify.py` prints the answer key | an empty or always-agreeing verifier proves nothing |
| the Auditor's `verify.py` tells the planted bug apart | the check only means something if the oracle disagrees with the bug |

The report lists the Auditor's verdicts in order, taken from what `ask` returned (a full-screen program redraws, so its screen at the end loses them), and how long each wait for an answer took. A run that passes with `REJECTED` before `APPROVED` is a real chain: delegate, produce, review, send back, fix, approve.

The report also counts messages sent to each teammate, so a run that only needed one round shows it.

## Scripted agents

`test/challenge/agents/` has a Maestro and a teammate written in bash. The Dev is wrong on purpose the first time. They prove that the harness, the chat, `recruit`, `ask`, `say` and the answer key work together, with no model, so `npm test` covers the challenge on every change.

## Free models

A run that hits a provider's limit stops at once with the outcome `provider-limit` (it looks for the messages agents print when a free tier ends), instead of waiting for the stall timeout. OpenRouter's free models allow 50 requests a day (1000 after a 10 dollar top-up), which one real run of the challenge can use up.

A real run passed on 2026-11-03: opencode with Nemotron 3 Ultra (free) as Maestro and gpt-oss-120b as teammates, 7 of 7 checks, 394 seconds, 9 messages, about 1.4 cents on OpenRouter. GLM 5.3 Flash as Maestro did not work: it treated the task as a bug report and asked the human a question instead of recruiting. Small models can fail the challenge for their own reasons; that says nothing about openmaestri.

OpenCode has free models (`opencode models`), but they stop with "Free usage limit reached" when the quota is used up. Since 0.21.4 openmaestri reports that at once instead of waiting for the timeout. Run the challenge when a probe such as `opencode run -m opencode/big-pickle "Reply OK"` answers.

## Gates in the challenge

The task text tells the Maestro to give the Dev `--check "python3 flag.py"` and to ask the Auditor with `--verdict` (see [checking work](validation.html)). The report counts the asks that the program judged and how many of them failed, next to the Auditor's verdicts, so a run shows whether the gate saved the Maestro from a mistake.

# Getting started

## First start: the welcome screen

The first time you open openmaestri with an empty canvas, a welcome window asks for two things: the **folder of your project** and the **agent** that will be your Maestro. The agents found on your machine come first and the first one is already selected, so for most people it is one click on **Start**.

It then opens that agent in a terminal inside your project folder, marked as the Maestro, so it can recruit and coordinate other agents. Ticking **Add an AGENTS.md** also writes a short instructions file for the agents (`CLAUDE.md` for Claude, `GEMINI.md` for Gemini). An existing file is never changed.

**Skip** closes the window for good. Nothing is shown when the workspace already has nodes, and `OPENMAESTRI_NO_WELCOME=1` turns the window off altogether.

## Install

**Debian / Ubuntu**

```bash
sudo apt install ./openmaestri_0.8.0_amd64.deb   # needs Node.js >= 22
openmaestri serve --open
```

If your distribution ships an older Node.js, install a current one from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org) or NodeSource first.

**From source**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri.git && cd openmaestri
npm ci          # needs build-essential and python3 (node-pty compiles)
npm start
```

The command prints a URL such as `http://127.0.0.1:7777/?token=...`. Open it once; the token is kept in a cookie. Running `openmaestri serve` again while it is already up just prints the URL again.

## Your first canvas

1. **Workspaces** live in the left sidebar. A workspace is a project directory with its own canvas. Create one with the **+** button.
2. **+ Terminal** opens a dialog. Pick a preset (a plain Shell is fine to start) and a directory.
3. **+ Note** adds a Markdown note. Notes are plain files under `~/.openmaestri/workspaces/<id>/notes/`.
4. **Pan** by dragging the background or scrolling. **Zoom** with Ctrl/Cmd + wheel, or the toolbar. **Fit** frames everything.
5. **Connect** two nodes with the ⚭ button on one, then click the other. Click a cable to remove it.

## Your first orchestration

1. Create a terminal, tick **Maestro**, and choose a preset such as *Maestro (OpenCode + DeepSeek)* (see [DeepSeek](deepseek.html)).
2. After the agent boots, openmaestri tells it to run `openmaestri guide`. Tell it your goal.
3. The Maestro recruits teammates (`openmaestri recruit`), which appear on the canvas already connected to it, and coordinates them with `ask`, `check` and shared notes.

You can try the whole mechanism without any API key: open two Shell terminals, connect them, and from one run `openmaestri ask "Shell 2" "echo hello"`.

## Where things are stored

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `~/.openmaestri/settings.json` | presets, roles, last workspace |
| `~/.openmaestri/workspaces/<id>/workspace.json` | nodes, connections, routines, viewport |
| `~/.openmaestri/workspaces/<id>/notes/*.md` | note bodies |
| `~/.openmaestri/env` | API keys as `KEY=VALUE` lines (keep it `chmod 600`) |
| `~/.openmaestri/token` | the UI token |

Set `OPENMAESTRI_DATA_DIR` to move all of it.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENMAESTRI_PORT` | `7777` | UI port on 127.0.0.1 (`0` = random) |
| `OPENMAESTRI_DATA_DIR` | `~/.openmaestri` | data root |
| `OPENMAESTRI_SOCKET_PATH` | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/openmaestri-<uid>/ipc.sock` | agent socket (must be under about 100 bytes) |

# Local CI

The GitHub workflows for CI and Security are disabled to save runner minutes. Everything they ran now runs on your machine with one script, when you ask for it.

```bash
scripts/check.sh               # quick: syntax, lint, the whole test suite (what a pull request needs)
scripts/check.sh --full        # quick + scripts/sast.sh + the .deb build and its smoke test
scripts/check.sh --dast        # also the dynamic tests (our attack checks and OWASP ZAP baseline, needs Docker)
scripts/check.sh --dast-full   # same, with the ZAP active scan (up to 10 minutes)
scripts/check.sh --matrix      # tests on Node 22 and 24, each in a clean copy (installs a missing version with nvm)
TAG=v1.2.3 scripts/check.sh --release   # version equals the tag, tests, .deb build and smoke test
```

Flags combine. Each step prints `ok` or `FAILED` with its time, a summary closes the run, and the exit code is 1 when any step failed.

| Step | Replaces |
|---|---|
| syntax, lint, tests | the `test` job of the CI workflow |
| `.deb` build and smoke test | the `deb` job |
| `scripts/sast.sh` | ESLint, `npm audit`, Semgrep, gitleaks and Trivy of the Security workflow (plus njsscan and shellcheck) |
| `scripts/dast.sh` | nothing before; it was already local only |
| `--matrix` | the Node 22 and 24 matrix |
| `--release` | the tag check of the Release workflow |

Two things are not replaced: **CodeQL** (no local run yet; Semgrep covers part of the same ground) and the **UI test's Chromium**, which the script installs once into `~/.cache/ms-playwright` when it is missing.

The suite starts many daemons and browsers at once. On a busy machine a timing-sensitive test can fail while it passes alone, so a failed file is rerun alone once. The summary prints `PASSED ON RERUN` when that happens; a real failure fails both times.

## Still on GitHub

The Release workflow still runs when you push a `v*` tag: it repeats the tests, builds the `.deb` and publishes the release (the only workflow that still spends minutes, and only on a tag). Dependabot keeps opening weekly update pull requests. To turn the CI and Security workflows back on: `gh workflow enable CI` and `gh workflow enable Security`.

# MCP servers and library documentation

Agents guess APIs when the model's training is older than the library. An MCP server such as **Context7** hands them the current documentation. openmaestri keeps one list of MCP servers for the workspace and writes it into the project config of the agents that read one, so every teammate starts with the same tools.

```bash
openmaestri mcp add context7                     # preset: current docs for libraries (remote, works without a key)
openmaestri mcp add context7 --key CONTEXT7_API_KEY   # with a key for higher limits (see below)
openmaestri mcp add tools --command "node tools/server.js" --env MODE=fast
openmaestri mcp                                  # list
openmaestri mcp install "Dev"                    # dry run: the diff of the file that would change
openmaestri mcp install "Dev" --apply            # write it (a backup is made first)
openmaestri mcp install "Dev" --remove --apply   # take them out again
openmaestri mcp rm tools
```

## Which agents

| Agent | File written in the agent's folder | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `.mcp.json` (`mcpServers`) | Claude asks you to approve each project server the first time |
| OpenCode | `opencode.json` (`mcp`) | `${VAR}` becomes `{env:VAR}`. A project with `opencode.jsonc` is left alone |

Codex, Goose and Gemini keep MCP servers in a global file, so openmaestri does not touch them. Other entries in the file are kept; only the servers of the workspace list are added, replaced or removed.

## Keys never go in the file

A header or environment value is plain text or exactly `${VAR}`. Anything that looks like a credential is refused. Put the key where your agents already get theirs, in `~/.openmaestri/env` (`CONTEXT7_API_KEY=...`, or `secret://` references, see [secrets](secrets.html)), and the placeholder is resolved when the agent starts.

## Safety

An MCP server is a program or a network service that your agent starts and trusts. So: only the Maestro adds or installs servers, a remote server must use `https` (plain `http` only for localhost) with no credentials in the URL, a local command is plain words with no shell, an install is a dry run until you pass `--apply`, nothing is written outside the workspace, and a symbolic link is never followed. If the file is committed, so is the server; read the diff.

The guide tells agents to use `context7`, when it is listed, before writing code against a library.
