# Which models work as Maestro

Real runs of the [orchestration challenge](functional-test.html), with a bug planted in the Dev's script (`--inject`), on 2026-11-04: three runs per Maestro, and six for the three that were run in both batches, 36 runs in all. The teammates were `gpt-oss-120b` in every run; only the Maestro changed. OpenCode, through OpenRouter. Three runs are enough to see that a model is unreliable, not to rank two close models.

| Maestro | Teammates | Runs | Passed | Stopped by a limit | Avg seconds | Avg messages | Repeated messages | Runs with a REJECTED | Median cost per pass |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| openrouter/anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 3 | 3 | 0 | 180 | 5.7 | 0 | 0 | $0.030 |
| openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 3 | 3 | 0 | 276 | 7.3 | 0 | 1 | $0.040 |
| openrouter/google/gemini-3.8-flash | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 3 | 3 | 0 | 448 | 5.0 | 0 | 0 | $0.310 |
| openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 3 | 3 | 0 | 229 | 5.0 | 0 | 0 | $0.070 |
| openrouter/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 6 | 5 | 0 | 317 | 5.2 | 1 | 0 | $0.040 |
| openrouter/openai/gpt-5.6-luna | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 3 | 2 | 0 | 236 | 8.3 | 0 | 1 | $0.030 |
| openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 6 | 3 | 0 | 361 | 6.3 | 2 | 2 | $0.045 |
| openrouter/nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 3 | 1 | 0 | 374 | 2.0 | 0 | 0 | - |
| openrouter/qwen/qwen3.7-flash | openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b | 6 | 1 | 0 | 639 | 12.3 | 7 | 1 | - |

"Runs with a REJECTED" counts runs where the Auditor refused the planted bug at least once (otherwise the program's own check caught it). A run passes when all 12 checks hold: the answer matches the key computed from the data, the script is right, the Maestro delegated instead of computing, the Maestro sent nothing twice, no figures were dictated to a teammate, and the planted bug was caught and fixed. "Median cost per pass" is what the agents' screens show as spent, over the runs that passed; it is empty for the cheap runs made before the column existed and for free models.

With three runs, 3 of 3 means anywhere from about 40% to 100%, 2 of 3 from about 20% to 95%, 1 of 3 from about 6% to 80%.

## What we saw

- **The slightly better models were steady.** Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Kimi K2.7 Code passed 3 of 3, gpt-5.6-luna 2 of 3. They all took the same path: about 5 messages, 3 program checks, no message twice, never asking the human.
- **More money did not buy more.** Gemini 3.8 Flash cost about ten times what Haiku 5.5 and gpt-5.6-luna cost per pass ($0.31 against $0.03) and was twice as slow. Haiku 5.5 and gpt-5.6-luna are the cheap end of the group that works.
- **A repeated-message failure was partly the harness, twice.** When a check kept failing the same way, the program sent its own correction to the Dev twice, and the harness counted that as the Maestro repeating itself; that is fixed and the first 24 runs were scored again. The harness also compared only the first 300 characters of each message, so two long messages that start alike counted as a repeat; that is fixed for new runs, and the old ones cannot be scored again because the full text was not kept. Read the "Repeated messages" column of the older runs as an upper bound.
- **The cheap group is noisy, not worse in one clear way.** The same four cheap Maestros, run again on code that differs only by a notice that never fired (see below), moved by a full run or more each: GLM 2 of 3 then 3 of 3, gpt-oss 1 of 3 then 2 of 3, Qwen 1 of 3 then 0 of 3. That is the size of the noise at three runs. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, new in the second batch, passed 3 of 3 at $0.04 per pass.
- **Qwen 3.7 Flash is the one that keeps failing.** 1 of 6 runs, 15 messages on average in the second batch and up to 18 minutes a run.
- **gpt-5.6-luna lost a run to a weak reviewer.** The Auditor (gpt-oss) refused a script the program's check accepted, and the Maestro spent 5 rounds and 13 messages before ending with `VERDICT: FAILED`. Failing closed was right; the loop was avoidable.
- **gpt-oss-120b as Maestro works about half the time** since the bootstrap names the program path (3 of 6; it delegated in every run).
- **Nemotron 3 Ultra (free) is inconclusive.** Two of its runs never started: the first prompt stayed QUEUED in OpenCode.
- A reviewer's `APPROVED` is cheap: in one run the Auditor approved a wrong list. What stopped it was the program comparing the Dev's script with an independent `verify.py` the Auditor wrote, not the Auditor's opinion. See [checking work](validation.html).

A second batch of cheap Maestros ran on a branch with one change: the first time the exact same message goes to a teammate, the Maestro is told how many seconds ago it sent it and that it was answered. The notice never fired in those 12 runs, so that batch measures the models again, not the notice, and the change was not merged. The repeats that did happen were not byte-for-byte copies (or, in older runs, only looked alike in their first 300 characters).

What to do with this: Haiku 5.5, gpt-5.6-luna, GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash are the ones to start with, all at 3 to 5 cents a pass; avoid Qwen 3.7 Flash and free models as Maestro. The gap between Qwen and the rest is the only one that three runs show clearly; the order of the others is not settled.

## The baseline: one agent alone

The same task given to one agent, with no Maestro, no Auditor, no `verify.py` and no gate (`--baseline`; it writes `flag.py` and an `answer.txt`). Five runs per model, on 2026-11-04, same OpenCode and OpenRouter. No bug is planted, since there is no hand-over to plant it in.

| Agent alone | Runs | Right answer | Avg seconds | Median cost per run |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 | 5 | 5 | 38 | not shown |
| deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash | 5 | 5 | 31 | not shown |
| moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code | 5 | 5 | 52 | $0.020 |
| openai/gpt-5.6-luna | 5 | 5 | 37 | $0.010 |
| openai/gpt-oss-120b | 5 | 5 | 51 | $0.010 |
| z-ai/glm-5.3-flash | 5 | 4 | 108 | not shown |

"Right answer" means the answer matches the key and `flag.py` prints it. The team runs above are judged by 12 checks, most of them about the way of working, so the fair comparison is on the right answer alone: the team got it in 31 of 36 runs, the single agent in 29 of 30 (the one miss was GLM stalling for 7 minutes). Cost is shown by OpenCode only on some runs; where it shows, the single agent spent 1 to 2 cents against 3 to 31 cents for the team.

What this says, and what it does not:

- **On this task the team did not buy a better answer.** One agent writes a 20-line script and checks it in under a minute, and gets it right as often as the team does, in a fifth to a tenth of the time and for a fraction of the money. `gpt-oss-120b` fails as a Maestro half the time but is 5 of 5 alone: the hard part for it is coordinating, not solving.
- **The task is small, and it has no trap for the single agent.** Nothing here shows what happens on work where one agent's script is wrong and nobody looks. The team's case is the independent check (the program compares the Dev's script with the Auditor's `verify.py`), and it was tested only by planting a bug for it to catch. A task where a lone agent errs often is needed to measure that, and the next step is to make one.
- **So the layer is for work a single agent gets wrong, not for every job.** Use a Maestro when a result must be checked by something other than the one who made it. For a task a single agent solves in a minute, send it to the agent.

## A second task, where the lone agent can fail (scenario B)

Scenario A is easy for a lone agent. Scenario B is a ledger with four traps: two ways of writing the amount (`1.250,50` and `1250.50`), two time zones, chargebacks that cancel a sale by reference (anywhere in the file), and repeated ids. The answer key of both data sets used (seeds 11 and 13) was checked against a second, independent reading of the file. The teammates were `gpt-oss-120b` in every team run; only the Maestro changed. A run counts when the final answer and the `flag.py` are both right.

| How the work was done | Qwen 3.7 Flash | gpt-oss-120b | DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One agent alone | 1 of 10 | 7 of 10 | 9 of 10 | 17 of 30 |
| Team, the Auditor's summary of the rules goes to the Dev (seed 11 only) | 1 of 5 | 3 of 5 | 3 of 5 | 7 of 15 |
| Team, the Dev reads the rule file itself | 6 of 8 | 3 of 10 | 10 of 10 | 19 of 28 |

Haiku 5.5 alone got 5 of 5 on seed 11. The Qwen team has 8 runs, not 10: the last two were cut to save time.

- **The team helps a weak solver and a good coordinator.** Qwen alone fails (1 of 10); led by Qwen, with the work done by `gpt-oss-120b`, the team got 6 of 8. DeepSeek alone is already good (9 of 10) and got 10 of 10 as the team's Maestro, above what the worker (`gpt-oss-120b`, 7 of 10 alone) does by itself. So a coordinator can lift a cheaper worker.
- **The team hurts when the Maestro is the weak link.** `gpt-oss-120b` alone got 7 of 10 and, as Maestro of the same worker, 3 of 10. The coordination added errors that its own solving did not have. Choosing the Maestro matters more than having one.
- **A summary is a lossy copy.** The challenge used to say "give the Dev the Auditor's rules in its own words". With four traps, the summary dropped some (the chargebacks and the time window were missing from the Dev's message in most failed runs) and the team did worse than the lone agents (7 of 15). Telling the Dev to read the file itself raised it. The Maestro's instructions now say to send sources and not summaries (rule 11), and `ask --relay` passes a reviewer's words on as written.
- **The team is slow.** A lone agent took about a minute; the team took 4 to 18 minutes.
- **Relaying the reviewer's words did not fix scenario A.** With `--relay` the three Maestros that fail most (gpt-oss, Qwen, gpt-5.6-luna) passed 9 of 15 runs, against 6 of 15 before, short of the 11 asked for. luna went 5 of 5; the other two did not move.
- **What this does not show.** Ten runs per cell on two data sets, one task of one kind, one worker model. The Qwen and gpt-oss differences are large enough to take seriously (Qwen 1 of 10 against 6 of 8, gpt-oss 7 of 10 against 3 of 10); the rest could be noise.

## Other workers, a Maestro with only the goal, and the state line (round 15)

Three questions asked after scenario B, answered with 30 real runs plus 8 controls (scenario B, seeds 11 and 13, a bug planted in the Dev's first script, "right" means the answer and the `flag.py` are both right).

**Does the team work with a worker other than `gpt-oss-120b`?** Maestro DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the Dev reads the files, `--relay`, four runs per worker:

| Worker | Right | Median cost per pass |
|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | 4 of 4 | $0.03 |
| Kimi K2.7 Code | 3 of 4 | $0.12 |
| GLM 5.3 Flash | 3 of 4 | $0.03 |
| `gpt-oss-120b` (the earlier table) | 10 of 10 | |

Yes. Neither miss was the team's coordination: one Kimi run stopped at an OpenCode permission question (the Maestro tried to write into `/usr/local/bin`) before any message to a teammate, and one GLM script was wrong. Kimi as a worker costs four times as much as the others for the same result.

**Can the Maestro build the plan itself?** The task is the goal only (`--free`): no steps, no roles, no gates, and the Maestro may read the files. The worker is `gpt-oss-120b`.

| Maestro | Right | Messages to teammates |
|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | 4 of 4 | 3 to 6 |
| Haiku 5.5 | 2 of 2 | 2 to 4 |
| Kimi K2.7 Code | 1 of 2 | 3 in the right run; the other worked alone, asked no teammate, and its answer never reached the human |
| `gpt-oss-120b` | 0 of 2 | one wrong script, one answer that never reached the human |

The two good Maestros recruited a reviewer and a Dev, asked for an independent check and got it right without being told how. The weak one still cannot. Eight runs is small, so read it as "it can", not as "it always does". The harness first let a Maestro wander out of the work folder and open the challenge's own files; the prompt now forbids it and a run that does so is not counted as right.

**Does a line written by the program help a weak Maestro?** With `OPENMAESTRI_STATE_LINE=1` every `ask` ends with one line the program writes from what it saw, for example `[openmaestri state] Dev: 2 messages, last check PASSED (python3 flag.py exit 0). Auditor: 1 message, last verdict REJECTED. Open: nothing.` `gpt-oss-120b` as Maestro of `gpt-oss-120b`, same code, same machine, same seeds:

| | Right | Passed (all 12 checks) | Seconds | Messages |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Without the line | 5 of 8 | 2 of 8 | 434 | 7.0 |
| With the line | 7 of 8 | 4 of 8 | 277 | 6.8 |

The direction is the one hoped for, but two runs of difference out of eight is inside the noise, so the line stays off by default. The 3 of 10 in the table above was measured with older code; the 5 of 8 of the control shows that the instructions and notes added since then, or luck, already moved this model. The verdict that kimi's plan asked to be "structured by the program" already was: the reviewer must end with `VERDICT: APPROVED or REJECTED - reason` and the program parses it, sends back once what does not parse and fails closed.

## Does the team beat one agent alone? Scenario C and the stop rule (round 16)

Three research rounds (Claude, kimi and agy, 2026-11-05, notes in `notes/planners/sintese15.md`) agreed on one mechanism that wins in the literature: two independent implementations compared by a program, with the reviewer blind to the other's code, and a lone-agent control with the same compute (a vote over several runs). Scenario C is the ledger of scenario B with a dial of 1 to 10 traps (number formats, time zones and a window, chargebacks, repeated ids, USD at 5.10 rounded half to even, partial refunds, VIP limits, weekend half, a cap per sale, small sales dropped). The key is checked in the tests against an independent Python reading with `Decimal`. The `--diff` mode has the Auditor write `verify.py` from the rules alone, the Dev write `flag.py`, and the Maestro run a `diff` of their outputs; it acts only when they differ.

The stop rule was set before the runs: the team has to beat the same model alone, with the same compute, by 20 points or more, on a task where the lone agent is under 50%.

Lone agent, 8 data sets per cell (right means the answer and `flag.py` are both right):

| Model | 4 traps | 6 traps | 7 traps | 10 traps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | 8 of 8 | 7 of 8 | 6 of 8 | 8 of 8 |
| GLM 5.3 Flash | | | 2 of 8 | |
| `gpt-oss-120b` | | | 2 of 8 | |

Seven traps, `gpt-oss-120b` (the model that fails alone):

| How the work was done | Right |
|---|---|
| One run alone | 14 of 40 (35%) |
| Majority vote over 4 runs, same data | 3 of 8 |
| Team: Maestro DeepSeek, Dev and Auditor `gpt-oss-120b`, the program compares two scripts | **6 of 8** |

- **The strong cheap model is not beaten.** DeepSeek V4.1 Flash alone got 8 of 8 even with ten traps (cost about a cent, about two minutes). The dial never took a strong model under 50%, so the rule cannot be met on this family of tasks: the team does not beat a strong model alone. If you can pay for one strong model, use one agent.
- **The team lifts a weak model, and it is not just more compute.** `gpt-oss-120b` alone is right in about a third of the runs; a vote over four runs does not help (3 of 8); the team, with a good Maestro and two independent scripts, is right in 6 of 8, as good as DeepSeek alone at seven traps (6 of 8). Against the 40 lone runs the difference has p of about 0.05 (Fisher, one side); against the vote, p of 0.16 with only eight data sets. Read it as a strong hint, not as proof.
- **What it costs.** A team run took one to four minutes and one to three cents (one run 16 cents); DeepSeek alone about a cent. The team only pays when the model you have to use is the weak one (open weights on your own machine, no access to a strong model).

## Seven agents instead of three (round 17)

The question left open by round 16: if two workers help a weak model, do six help more? Seven agents is a Maestro (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) and six workers (`gpt-oss-120b`) who each write their own script from the rules; the Maestro runs all six and takes the biggest group of identical outputs, at least three scripts and bigger than every other group (`run.mjs --wide 6`). Same eight data sets as the trio (scenario C, seven traps, seeds 21 to 701), 2026-11-06, one run at a time. Raw lines in `notes/runs-round17/wide6.jsonl`.

| Team | Right | Seconds | Messages | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maestro + Dev + Auditor (the trio) | **6 of 8** | one to four minutes | | 1 to 3 cents |
| Maestro + 6 workers (seven agents) | 4 of 8 | 363 on average | 12 to 21 | 1 to 19 cents (shown on 6 of 8 runs) |

- **More agents did not help; the direction is against it.** The seven were right at seeds 21, 101, 401 and 501 and wrong at 201, 301, 601 and 701. The trio was wrong at 301 and 701 only. Four against six out of eight is inside the noise (Fisher, one side, p about 0.3), so read it as "no gain shown, and no reason to expect one", not as proof that seven is worse.
- **Plurality of weak scripts may not be independence.** `gpt-oss-120b` is right about a third of the time alone, and its mistakes need not be scattered: six copies of one model can share the same blind spot and agree on a wrong answer. The final answer was wrong at seeds 201, 301 and 601; I did not read the six scripts of those runs to see whether the biggest group was wrong or the Maestro misjudged the groups, so this is a likely reason and not a finding. The trio compares a script with one written to a different brief (the Auditor's `verify.py` from the rules alone) and acts on the difference.
- **Failures were not all about the answer.** Seed 701 stalled with no message sent: the Maestro never recruited anyone. Seed 201 also had an agent open the challenge's own files. Seven terminals cost more time (about six minutes a run on average, against one to four for the trio) and more messages for a Maestro to hold.
- **Self-test.** `openmaestri selftest --runs 1 --traps 4` on the same machine with the starter team: right, 299 seconds, 11 messages, 3 cents.

Stop rule from round 16: more agents have to beat the trio by 20 points. They did not (they were 25 points under), so the starter team stays at three, and the research on team size ends here. What stays open is not research but use: the team helps when the model you have to use is weak, and a strong cheap model alone (DeepSeek, 8 of 8 at ten traps) is as good.
- **The two misses of the team**, read in the logs: on seed 701 both scripts agreed (the diff printed `SAME`) on an answer with one name too many, so the program had nothing to compare; that is the error two independent writers share, which the N-version literature predicts and a diff cannot see. On seed 301 the scripts never agreed in four rounds (eleven messages, 16 cents), and the Maestro answered with a list that matches neither script, `Centro,Leste,Litoral,Norte,Sul`, after saying the rule text decided for the Auditor's script: the arbitration step in the Maestro's instructions is the weak part.
- **The weak Maestro is still the weak link:** every team here had a good Maestro (DeepSeek). The earlier tables show what a weak one does.

# One-shot agents

`openmaestri agent <driver> "prompt"` gives a question or a job to an agent CLI in its **non-interactive mode** and prints the answer. There is no terminal on the canvas and no screen to read: the process starts, answers, and is gone. It is the simple way for a Maestro to use a second opinion, a cheaper model for a small job, or several agents at once.

```bash
openmaestri agent claude "Summarise the open TODOs in @file:TODO.md"
openmaestri agent opencode-deepseek "Write a unit test for src/files.js" --floor feature-x
openmaestri agent agy "Review this plan" --model gemini-3.8-flash --timeout 5m
```

Only a Maestro can run it. The agent works in the Maestro's folder, or in a floor with `--floor`. `@agent:`, `@note:` and `@file:` mentions in the prompt are expanded the same way as in the chat.

## One task, several agents

```bash
openmaestri run "Find the bug in the login flow" --agents claude,opencode-deepseek,agy --dry-run
openmaestri run "Find the bug in the login flow" --agents claude,opencode-deepseek,agy --floors
```

Every agent gets the same task and they run in parallel (2 to 6 of them). The answer of each one is quoted as it came, with its status and time, in one report. The report is printed and also left as a note next to the Maestro. Nothing summarises it with a model, so it never invents or loses a result; a failing agent is marked and the others still count (the command only fails when all of them fail).

- `--dry-run` shows what would run (agents, folders, floors) and starts nothing. It still checks that every driver exists and its program is installed.
- `--floors` gives each agent its own floor: a separate git worktree and branch, so they cannot overwrite each other. It needs the workspace folder to be a git repository. A snapshot of each floor is taken when its agent finishes, so `openmaestri floor rollback NAME ID` puts back what the agent produced after you change files by hand. Floors are kept for you to review; land the one you want with `openmaestri floor land NAME`, and remove the others with `openmaestri floor delete NAME`. Without `--floors` all agents share one folder, which is fine for questions and reviews and risky for edits.
- `--model M` applies to every driver that takes a model, `--timeout 10m` to each agent.

## Drivers

Any agent works; DeepSeek is only the pair of cheapest presets.

| Driver | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `claude` | `claude -p PROMPT [--model M]` |
| `codex` | `codex exec --skip-git-repo-check [--model M] PROMPT` (read-only sandbox by default: it answers and reviews, it does not edit files) |
| `gemini` | `gemini [--model M] -p PROMPT` |
| `agy` | `agy -p PROMPT [--model M]` (Antigravity) |
| `kimi` | `kimi -p PROMPT [--model M]` |
| `opencode` | `opencode run [-m M] PROMPT` |
| `aider` | `aider --message PROMPT --yes-always --no-auto-commits --no-pretty --no-gitignore --no-analytics --no-check-update --no-show-release-notes` with its chat and input history sent to `/dev/null`, `[--model M]`. Outside a git repository aider creates one, and it leaves a `.aider.tags.cache.v4` file |
| `goose` | `goose run --no-session -q [--provider P --model M] -t PROMPT`; `--model openai/gpt-5` gives both, a bare model uses `GOOSE_PROVIDER` |
| `opencode-deepseek`, `aider-deepseek` | the two above with `deepseek/<model>` (`OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL`, default `deepseek-flash`) |

Status of each driver, checked against the real program (2026-11-02, the last four on a clean Ubuntu 24.04 machine):

| Driver | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `claude`, `kimi`, `agy` | run end to end: the answer comes back, the exit code and time are reported |
| `gemini` | flags match `gemini --help`; the run needs a Gemini account that is still supported (Google ended the CLI for individual accounts and points to Antigravity, so use `agy`) |
| `codex`, `opencode`, `goose`, `aider` | checked with the real programs (codex 0.166, opencode 1.19, goose 1.57, aider 0.86): all four give a full answer through OpenRouter (`openai/gpt-oss-120b`, 2026-11-03). For codex set `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL` (openmaestri passes the key as `CODEX_API_KEY` and the endpoint as `-c openai_base_url`); for goose use `--model openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b` |

What the real programs taught the drivers: `codex` refuses to start outside a git repository without `--skip-git-repo-check`; `goose` aborts without a model; `aider` exits 0 when the provider refuses the call (openmaestri now reports that as a failure) and writes history files into the folder (now sent to `/dev/null`); `opencode` prints colour codes even with `NO_COLOR` (removed from reports).

Run `openmaestri doctor` to see which programs are installed on your machine. If a flag of yours differs, override the driver as shown below.

These flags are what each tool documents today. When a tool changes them, or you want another tool, add or override a driver in `~/.openmaestri/settings.json`:

```json
{ "drivers": { "claude": { "bin": "claude", "args": ["-p", "{prompt}", "--model", "{model}"] },
               "mytool": { "bin": "mytool", "args": ["--ask", "{prompt}"] } } }
```

`{prompt}` is required and is always a single argument; no shell is involved, so a prompt cannot run commands. A driver that does not show up in `openmaestri agent` is missing `{prompt}` or has a name outside lowercase letters, digits and `-`.

## When an account runs out of quota

Free tiers and prepaid credit end. When a one-shot run fails because the account is out of quota, credit or rate allowance (the message says "usage limit", "quota", "429", "credit balance" and the like), openmaestri can hand the same prompt to the next driver:

```bash
openmaestri fallback set opencode kimi,agy      # saved: opencode, then kimi, then agy
openmaestri agent opencode "..."                # uses the saved chain
openmaestri agent opencode "..." --fallback agy # or a chain for this call only
openmaestri fallback list | fallback clear opencode
```

The answer ends with a line such as `[kimi, 12.4s, project, skipped opencode (Free usage limit reached)]`, so you always see who answered. A driver that refused is not tried again for 30 minutes. Only the quota case triggers this: a task that fails for another reason fails, it is not passed on. The model and the account of the first driver are not carried over, since they belong to it. `run --agents` never swaps one agent for another: every agent in that list is there on purpose.

## In a container

`--sandbox IMAGE` runs the agent inside a Docker container instead of directly on your machine:

```bash
openmaestri agent claude "Review src/" --sandbox my-agents:latest
openmaestri run "Find the bug" --agents claude,codex --floors --sandbox my-agents:latest --no-network
```

You provide the image: it must contain the agent program (`claude`, `aider`...). openmaestri then runs it with:

- only the working folder shared, at `/work`, writable; nothing else of your machine is visible (not your home folder, not your keys);
- your user id, not root; all Linux capabilities dropped; no privilege gain; 2 GB of memory and 256 processes at most;
- the variables the driver is allowed (see below) passed **by name**, so values never appear in a process list;
- `--no-network` removes the network entirely (useful for review jobs that need no API);
- the container is killed on timeout or cancel, not just the `docker` client.

If Docker is not running, you are not allowed to use it, or the image is missing, the message says which and what to do.

A custom driver can carry its own sandbox in `settings.json`: `"sandbox": { "image": "my-agents:latest", "network": "none", "memory": "1g" }`. Programs that sign in through files in your home folder (for example a logged-in `claude`) do not find them inside the container; give them a key through an [account](accounts.html) instead.

## A teammate in a box

A one-shot run can be boxed (above). So can a terminal teammate:

```bash
openmaestri recruit "Worker" --preset "OpenCode" --sandbox my-agents:latest [--no-network]
```

The agent runs in a container with a terminal, from an image that has the agent installed. It sees only its folder (mounted at `/work`), has no capabilities, no new privileges, 2 GB of memory, no daemon socket and no `OPENMAESTRI_*` variables, so it cannot drive the canvas: the Maestro talks to it with `ask` and `check` as always. Only the keys of the teammate's account are passed in, by name. When the agent ends, the pane ends: there is no host shell behind it. Closing or restarting the pane removes the container.

The Maestro itself cannot be boxed, since it has to reach the app, and a plain shell cannot either. Persistent (tmux) sessions are not used for boxed terminals.

## Safety

- **Keys per driver.** A driver is given only the secret variables it needs: `claude` gets the Anthropic key, `aider-deepseek` the DeepSeek key, and neither sees the other. Settings that are not secrets (such as `OPENMAESTRI_DEEPSEEK_MODEL`) pass to all. A custom driver lists its own with `"keys": ["MY_TOKEN"]`; without that list it receives every key in the env file, since you wrote the driver.
- **No planted programs.** The program is found through your own shell, and a program that resolves inside the workspace or a floor (also through a symbolic link) is refused, so a repository cannot shadow `claude` by putting a file of that name on `PATH`.
- **No keyring, no agent socket.** The desktop keyring bus, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` and the display are not passed on, so a one-shot agent cannot ask the keyring for your other secrets or use your SSH agent.

- The program starts with a short allow-list of your environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, locale, proxies, certificates) plus the keys from `~/.openmaestri/env` (including `secret://` ones). It never receives `OPENMAESTRI_*`, so it cannot drive the canvas, and it does not see other tokens in the daemon's environment.
- Standard input is closed: a tool that asks a question gets end-of-file instead of hanging.
- A time limit (default 10 minutes, at most 60) stops the agent and every process it started. At most 6 run at once. Output is cut at 400 KB.
- What this does not do: without `--sandbox` it is not a sandbox. An agent runs as you, so it can still read your home folder, use your git credentials stored in files, and start a background process that escapes the time limit (`setsid`, `nohup`). A floor separates the working files, not the shared `.git` folder. For code you do not trust, run openmaestri inside a container or a virtual machine.

# Persistent terminals

Normally, stopping openmaestri stops its terminals. With persistence on, each terminal runs inside its own **tmux** session, so an agent that is in the middle of a long job keeps working while you restart openmaestri, update it, or reboot the page. When openmaestri starts again it attaches to the same sessions: the command is not run a second time.

## Turn it on

```bash
sudo apt install tmux
OPENMAESTRI_PERSIST=tmux openmaestri        # for one run
```

or tick **Keep terminals running when openmaestri restarts** in *Preferences* (command palette), which writes `"persistTerminals": true` to `~/.openmaestri/settings.json` and takes effect the next time openmaestri starts. `openmaestri doctor` shows whether tmux is found.

## How it behaves

- Closing the page or reloading it never stopped anything; this is about stopping and starting **openmaestri itself**.
- **Dismissing** a terminal, deleting its node, unloading a workspace or removing a floor ends its session for good. Only a plain shutdown of openmaestri leaves sessions running.
- Sessions of terminals that were deleted while openmaestri was stopped are removed at the next start.
- It uses a private tmux server (socket `openmaestri`, no config file, no status bar, no prefix key), so your own tmux is not touched. `tmux -L openmaestri ls` lists the sessions.
- Each session gets the environment it was created with (keys from `~/.openmaestri/env`, accounts), and the tmux server itself starts with an almost empty environment, so one terminal's keys never reach another. Values never appear on a command line.
- A terminal whose agent had exited before the restart comes back as the shell it fell back to, and chat messages are not typed into it.
- Scrolling back happens in tmux's own history, not in the canvas scrollback of a freshly attached terminal, which starts from the screen as tmux redraws it.
- If tmux is missing or fails, terminals start as plain ones and a warning is logged.

## See them, end them

```bash
openmaestri persist list          # each session: terminal id, since when, what runs in it
openmaestri persist stop --yes    # end all of them (and the programs in them)
openmaestri ps                    # terminals kept in tmux are marked
openmaestri doctor                # how many sessions are running now
```

Sessions keep using memory after you quit, on purpose; this is how you check on them. `persist` runs only in your own shell, never inside an agent terminal.

# Portals

A portal is a web page on the canvas that **both you and your agents can drive**. It is a real Chromium running on your machine, shown as a live view; you click and type in it, and agents use `openmaestri portal ...` on the same page.

## Requirements

Chrome or Chromium on the machine that runs openmaestri (`apt install chromium`, or Google Chrome). openmaestri looks in the usual places; set `OPENMAESTRI_CHROME=/path/to/chrome` to choose one. Without a browser, a portal falls back to a plain sandboxed iframe: you can look at the page, but agents cannot act on it, and many sites refuse to be framed.

In containers where Chrome's own sandbox cannot start, set `OPENMAESTRI_CHROME_NO_SANDBOX=1` (this weakens the browser's isolation; do not browse untrusted sites that way).

## The agent loop

```bash
openmaestri portal create http://localhost:3000 "App"
openmaestri portal snapshot "App"          # the page as an accessibility tree, with @refs
openmaestri portal fill "App" @e2 "ada@example.com"
openmaestri portal click "App" @e5
openmaestri portal wait "App" "#dashboard" 8000
openmaestri portal text "App" "#dashboard h1"
openmaestri portal screenshot "App"        # prints the path of a PNG
```

`snapshot` prints one line per useful element:

```
page: Sign in  http://localhost:3000/login
heading "Sign in" [level=1]
@e1 heading "Sign in" ...
@e2 textbox "Email" value=""
@e3 textbox "Password" [required]
@e4 checkbox "Remember me"
@e5 button "Sign in" [disabled]
```

A **target** is `@e3` (from the last snapshot), a CSS selector, or `x,y` page pixels. References belong to one snapshot: after the page navigates they are rejected with "run `portal snapshot` again", so an agent never clicks the wrong element.

## Commands

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `portal create URL ["Name"] [--size WxH]` | New portal wired to you (http and https only) |
| `portal edit "P" --url URL` · `portal close "P"` | Navigate · remove (the browser is closed) |
| `snapshot` (alias `a11y`) | Accessibility tree with `@e` references |
| `click` · `hover` · `drag A B` | Mouse actions on a target |
| `fill T "text"` · `type "text"` · `clear [T]` | Set a field (fires `input`/`change`) · type into the focused element · empty a field |
| `key "Enter"` | Key press; modifiers as in `ctrl+a`, `cmd+c`, `shift+tab`; also F1-F12, arrows, Home/End |
| `focus T` · `selectall [T]` · `select T "Option"` | Focus, select text, pick a `<select>` option by its text |
| `check [T]` · `uncheck T` | Tick or clear a checkbox (`check` with no target takes a screenshot) |
| `navigate "url"` · `back` · `forward` · `reload` | History |
| `scroll down 300 [T]` · `scrollintoview T` | Scroll the page, or the container under a target |
| `text T` · `html` · `info` | Read element text, page HTML (cut at 200 KB), url/title/viewport |
| `wait T [ms]` | Wait until a target is on the page and visible (default 5000 ms) |
| `evaluate "js"` | Run JavaScript in the page and print the result as JSON |
| `logs-start` · `logs` | Capture console output and page errors, then read and clear them |
| `screenshot` | PNG saved under `~/.openmaestri/portals/<id>/` (the last 20 are kept) |
| `resize W H` · `ua [preset]` | Exact viewport in CSS pixels · `ios`, `android`, `chrome`, `edge`, `firefox`, `desktop` |
| `upload T file...` | Fill a file input; files must be inside the workspace or a floor |

Android device portals (`portal devices`, `tap`, `swipe`, ...) are not implemented yet.

## What a portal can and cannot do

- Only **http and https** pages open. `file:`, `chrome:`, `devtools:`, `view-source:`, `ftp:` and `javascript:` are refused for agents and blocked inside the browser (a page that redirects to `file:///etc/passwd` stays where it was).
- Cloud **metadata and link-local addresses** (`169.254.0.0/16`, `metadata.google.internal`, and the Azure and Alibaba equivalents) and openmaestri's **own control port** are refused, both when you type them and when a page tries to reach them. Other `localhost` ports stay open: testing your dev server is what portals are for. `localhost:3000` and `example.com` need no `http://`.
- Each portal has its **own temporary profile**: no cookies or logins from your normal browser, and nothing is kept after the portal closes.
- The browser is controlled over a **pipe**, not a TCP debugging port, so no other process can attach to it.
- Pages that open new windows are kept in the same portal; dialogs (`alert`, `confirm`) are answered automatically.
- A portal's browser is shut down when its node is deleted, when openmaestri stops, or after 15 idle minutes with nobody viewing it; it restarts at the last URL on the next use.
- `evaluate` and `upload` act with your privileges inside the page and on the workspace folder. Treat agents that browse untrusted sites like you would any automation: prompt injection through page content is possible (see [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/blob/main/SECURITY.md)).

# Project memory

Chat memory (see [chat](chat.html)) keeps one conversation readable. **Project memory** keeps what the *project* learned, so an agent that starts tomorrow does not repeat what an agent did yesterday: decisions ("we use pnpm, not npm"), lessons ("port 3000 is taken by the mock"), facts.

```bash
openmaestri remember "Use pnpm, not npm" --kind decision      # any agent
openmaestri facts                                             # list, newest last
openmaestri facts search pnpm
openmaestri facts rm 3fa91c                                   # Maestro only
openmaestri facts export "Dev"                                # dry run: what would go into Dev's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md
openmaestri facts export "Dev" --apply                        # write it between markers, with a backup
```

## What fills it

- **You and your agents**, with `remember`. The guide tells agents to read `facts` before planning and to save decisions and traps.
- **openmaestri itself**, one line when a floor is landed or a `run` finishes. These are marked `(auto)`, are dropped first when the list is full (200 entries), and are not exported.

## Who sees it

A new teammate (`recruit`) and a replacement (`recruit --replace`) are told how many entries there are and shown the newest decisions, as information and not as orders. The Maestro gets the same when it starts. The full list is one command away.

## Safety

Everything one agent writes is read by others, so entries are one line (400 characters), credentials are masked, and leading `#`, `>` and `-` are stripped so an entry cannot pose as a heading or a list of orders. Entries live in the data folder of the workspace, not in your repository, until you export them.

`facts export` uses the same marker block, backup and workspace-only rule as roles ([agents](agents.html)).

# How to report a bug

Good reports get fixed fast. It takes about five minutes.

1. **Search first.** Look through [open and closed issues](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/issues?q=is%3Aissue) for the same symptom.
2. **Update.** Make sure you are on the latest [release](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/releases/latest) or `main`.
3. **Collect diagnostics.** In the affected terminal run:
   ```bash
   openmaestri debug
   openmaestri version
   node --version
   uname -a
   ```
4. **Find a minimal reproduction.** Ideally with a plain Shell terminal instead of a paid agent: `openmaestri ask "Shell 2" "echo hi"` is easier for us to reproduce than a long agent session.
5. **Open the issue** with [this form](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/issues/new?template=bug_report.yml). Fill in what you expected, what happened, steps, and the diagnostics.
6. **Redact secrets.** Never paste API keys, tokens (the `?token=` part of the UI URL), or private code. If a log may contain them, trim it.

## Security problems

Do **not** open a public issue for a vulnerability. Use [private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/security/advisories/new). See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

## Feature ideas and questions

Use the [feature request form](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/issues/new?template=feature_request.yml) for ideas, and [Discussions](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/discussions) for questions.

## What happens next

A maintainer will label the issue (`bug`, `needs-info`, `good first issue`, `help wanted`). If it is labelled `help wanted`, you are welcome to fix it: see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

# API keys and secrets

openmaestri works with any command line agent: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Aider, Goose, or whatever you add as a preset. DeepSeek has ready-made presets and prices because it is the cheapest way to run many agents, not because it is the only choice. Every key an agent needs is a plain environment variable, and the terminal starts with the ones you list in `~/.openmaestri/env`:

```
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...      # Claude Code
OPENAI_API_KEY=...         # Codex, Aider, OpenCode
GEMINI_API_KEY=...         # Gemini CLI
DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...       # OpenCode and Aider with DeepSeek
```

## Keep the key out of that file

Store it once and point to it:

```bash
openmaestri secrets set anthropic        # type it (hidden), or: pass it on stdin
echo 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=secret://anthropic' >> ~/.openmaestri/env
```

`secret://anthropic` is replaced by the stored value when a terminal starts. A reference to a secret that is not stored is left out (and a warning tells you the command to fix it); the reference text is never handed to the agent as if it were the key.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `openmaestri secrets set NAME` | Store a value. Read from stdin or typed with the echo off, never an argument (it would show in `ps` and your shell history). |
| `openmaestri secrets list` | Names only. |
| `openmaestri secrets status` | Which backend is in use. |
| `openmaestri secrets rm NAME` | Forget one. |

Names are lowercase letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore.

## Where the value lives

- **keyring**: the desktop keyring through `secret-tool` (`apt install libsecret-tools`), used automatically when it works (looked up in /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin and /bin only; `OPENMAESTRI_SECRET_TOOL=/abs/path` overrides).
- **file**: `~/.openmaestri/secrets.json`, mode 0600, used when there is no usable keyring (a server, a container). It has the same trust level as the env file it replaces, so this is not encryption: openmaestri does not invent a home-made cipher whose key would sit next to the data.

`OPENMAESTRI_SECRETS_BACKEND=file|keyring|auto` forces a choice.

## What it protects

- The `secrets` command refuses to run inside an agent terminal, so an agent cannot read or change your keys through openmaestri.
- Secrets are never in `workspace.json`, an export, the chat memory, the usage log or `doctor` output.
- This does not stop a program that runs as you from reading your files. Give an agent only the key it needs, and use separate keys with spending limits where the provider allows it.

`openmaestri doctor` shows the backend and how many secrets are stored, and checks that a `secret://` key resolves, without printing it.

# Security scanning

The checks run on your machine, not on GitHub (see [local-ci.md](local-ci.md)). One command runs every static-analysis tool:

```bash
scripts/sast.sh
```

| Tool | What it checks | Where |
|---|---|---|
| ESLint + `eslint-plugin-security` + `no-unsanitized` | unsafe patterns, regex DoS, `child_process`, DOM sinks | `npm run lint` |
| Semgrep (javascript, nodejs, security-audit, owasp-top-ten, secrets, command-injection, xss, github-actions) | taint and misuse rules, workflow hardening | local |
| njsscan | Node.js specific rules | local |
| CodeQL (`security-extended`) | data-flow analysis | not local yet (the old workflow is disabled); Semgrep covers part of it |
| gitleaks | secrets in the tree and in git history | local |
| Trivy | vulnerable dependencies, secrets, misconfiguration | local |
| `npm audit` | known advisories, including dev dependencies | local |
| shellcheck | the shell scripts (packaging, shims, fixtures) | local |
| ruff, bandit | Python (there is none today; enabled automatically if any appears) | local |

GitHub Actions are pinned to commit SHAs and Dependabot proposes updates with a 7-day cooldown. `.npmrc` sets `min-release-age=7` so freshly published packages are not installed immediately.

## Dynamic tests (DAST)

Static analysis reads the code; these attack a running daemon.

```bash
scripts/dast.sh            # our attack checks, then the OWASP ZAP baseline (needs Docker)
scripts/dast.sh --no-zap   # only our checks
scripts/dast.sh --full     # our checks, then the ZAP active scan (up to 10 minutes)
```

`test/dast.mjs` starts the real daemon in a temporary data folder and sends it what an attacker would: no token, a wrong token, a forged cookie, foreign `Host` and `Origin` headers (DNS rebinding, `Origin: null`), path traversal in every route, odd HTTP methods, 200 KB URLs and 100 KB headers, a request-smuggling attempt, a half-open connection, and on the WebSocket a foreign origin, hostile messages (`null`, prototype keys), and a frame over the 8 MB limit. It also checks the headers and the CSP, that the port listens on `127.0.0.1` only, and the modes of the data folder, token file and agent socket. It fails if the daemon dies at any point.

The ZAP baseline is a passive scan plus a spider with the token in the URL. It reports four warnings that are the design, not defects: the token cookie (session management), `Cache-Control: no-store` (non-storable content), the token in the first URL (printed once, then the browser is redirected to `/` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` keeps it out of other sites), and the cookie being set from that URL (it only happens when the value already equals the real token).

The first run of these checks found three ways to stop the daemon, now fixed and covered by `test/security.test.js`: an `Origin: null` header (what a sandboxed frame on any web page sends), a WebSocket message that is JSON `null`, and a WebSocket frame over the size limit.

## Two noisy ESLint rules are off, on purpose

`security/detect-non-literal-fs-filename` and `security/detect-object-injection` fire on every dynamic path or property access and cannot tell safe from unsafe. The risks they stand for are handled in code and covered by `test/security.test.js`:

- ids that become file names go through `safeId()` and must be canonical UUIDs
- lookups keyed by external input use `Object.hasOwn` (commands, node kinds, MIME types, vendor paths)
- node fields from the UI are type- and range-checked before they are stored

## Accepted risks

- `routine create --pre-run` runs a user-written shell command in the daemon. It has the same privileges as the terminals, a 60 s timeout and a 1 MiB output cap, and is marked with an `eslint-disable` that explains why.
- Agents run with your privileges. See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/baduba/openmaestri/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

| **Starter Dev (gpt-oss-120b)** | `openai/gpt-oss-120b` | The worker in every team run: 10 of 10 on the first ledger task. Almost free |

Left out on purpose: Kimi K2.7 Code (3 of 4 as a worker, four times the cost), GLM 5.3 Flash (3 of 4), gpt-5.6-luna (2 of 3 as Maestro), Gemini 3.8 Flash (3 of 3 but ten times the cost), Qwen 3.7 Flash and the free models (they fail).

Each model can be changed with a variable in `~/.openmaestri/env`: `OPENMAESTRI_STARTER_MAESTRO`, `OPENMAESTRI_STARTER_DEV`, `OPENMAESTRI_STARTER_AUDITOR`, and `OPENMAESTRI_STARTER_MAESTRO_ALT` / `OPENMAESTRI_STARTER_DEV_ALT` for the two extra presets (a model id as OpenRouter writes it; `opencode models openrouter` lists them).

## Set it up

```bash
install -m 600 /dev/null ~/.openmaestri/env          # skip if the file exists
echo 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-your-key' >> ~/.openmaestri/env
opencode auth login        # choose OpenRouter, paste the key
openmaestri doctor         # tells you what is still missing
```

In the New terminal dialog choose **Starter Maestro (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash)**. Then tell it what you want and how to use the team, for example:

> Goal: (what you want built or found). Use the presets "Starter Dev (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash)" and "Starter Auditor (gpt-oss-120b)". The Auditor writes a check from the spec alone, without seeing the Dev's code. The Dev writes the code. The program decides: run both and compare their outputs (or run the Auditor's tests with `--check`). You act only when they differ, at most 4 rounds. Never retell the spec or a reply: send the file path and use `--relay`.

## What we measured, and what we did not

Everything below is in [which models work](models.html), with the runs.

- **The Maestro** is the weak link. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Haiku 5.5, Kimi K2.7 Code and gpt-5.6-luna led teams that passed; `gpt-oss-120b`, Qwen 3.7 Flash and the free models were poor Maestros. That is why the Maestro here is DeepSeek.
- **The workers can be cheap.** With a DeepSeek Maestro, `gpt-oss-120b` workers were right in 10 of 10 runs on the first ledger task and in 6 of 8 on the harder one (ten rules with traps), where `gpt-oss-120b` alone was right in 14 of 40 runs and a vote over four runs in 3 of 8. DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM workers were right in 4 of 4, 3 of 4 and 3 of 4. The Auditor is a different model family from the Dev so that their mistakes are less likely to be the same.
- **A strong cheap model alone is as good.** DeepSeek V4.1 Flash alone was right in 8 of 8 runs even with ten traps, for about a cent. If you can use it alone, use one agent. The team pays when the model you have to use is a weak one (open weights on your own machine, a strict budget, no strong model).
- **More agents did not help.** A Maestro and six `gpt-oss-120b` workers, taking the biggest group of identical scripts, were right in 4 of 8 runs on the hard task, against 6 of 8 for the trio on the same data, and slower. Their mistakes are alike, so a larger vote does not separate them. Keep the trio. Details in [which models work](models.html), round 17.
- **Not tested: other kinds of work.** The runs are one family of tasks (read a ledger, apply rules, print a list). The starter team is a good place to begin, not a promise for any code.
- **The cross-family choice of the Auditor is a hunch,** supported by the literature on correlated errors but not measured against a Dev and Auditor of the same model here.

Check that the team works on your machine, with your key and your models: `openmaestri selftest` runs the ledger challenge (ten-rule scenario, seven traps) twice and says how many runs were right; `openmaestri selftest --solo` does the same with the Maestro model alone, so you see whether you need the team at all. Two runs show that it can work, not that it always does: use `--runs 6` before trusting it.

A run costs a few cents. Set a limit before you start: `OPENMAESTRI_BUDGET_USD=1 openmaestri serve` (see [validation](validation.html)).

# Troubleshooting

Run `openmaestri doctor` first: it checks Node, git, the browser, the agents, your DeepSeek key and the data folder, and prints the fix for anything missing. Then `openmaestri debug` inside the affected terminal. It prints the daemon uptime, socket, workspace, terminal id and what that terminal can reach.

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `only available inside openmaestri terminals` | You ran the command in a normal shell. Open a terminal from the canvas. |
| `cannot reach the openmaestri daemon` | The app is not running, or the socket path differs. Run `openmaestri serve`. |
| `no terminal named "X" is connected to you` | Connect them (⚭ button, or `connect` from a Maestro). The message lists what you can reach. |
| `only available to Maestro terminals` | Recreate the terminal with **Maestro** ticked, or pick a Maestro preset. |
| `403 forbidden` in the browser | Open the exact URL printed by `openmaestri serve` (it has the token). |
| `socket path is too long` | Set `OPENMAESTRI_SOCKET_PATH` to a shorter path (limit about 100 bytes). |
| `openmaestri is already running` | One daemon per user. The URL is printed again; open it. |
| Terminal output looks garbled after zoom | Reset zoom with the percentage button; the terminal refits on resize. |
| `ask` returns too early or late | Use `--timeout 5m` and `check` to see the live screen. |
| DeepSeek preset says `command not found` | Install `opencode` or `aider` and make sure it is on `PATH` for your login shell. |
| `npm ci` fails building node-pty | Install `build-essential` and `python3`. |
| `N terminals are already running (the limit is 40)` | Close terminals, or raise `OPENMAESTRI_MAX_TERMINALS` |
| `"opencode" was not found in your shell` | Install the agent. `openmaestri doctor` lists what is missing and how to install it |
| Port 7777 in use | `OPENMAESTRI_PORT=0 openmaestri serve` picks a free port. |

Still stuck? [Report a bug](reporting-bugs.html).

# What "done" means for the validation layer

The layer is the part of openmaestri that judges work with the program instead of the model: `ask --check`, `--verdict`, `--then`, the loop guard, the Maestro watchdog, the report, the budget and `resume`. This page says when it counts as finished, and where it stands on 2026-11-04.

| Criterion | State |
|---|---|
| A failed check goes back to the teammate by itself, capped, with a clipped log | Done, tested |
| A verdict that is missing or malformed fails closed | Done, tested |
| The answer to the human says when a check was left failing | Done, tested |
| A reviewer's REJECTED against a passing check is flagged to the Maestro | Done, released in 0.25.0 |
| A loop of similar messages is warned at the 3rd and refused at the 5th | Done, tested |
| A Maestro that stops answering is reminded, at most twice | Done, tested |
| A spending limit stops terminals and one-shot agents, set only by the person | Done. Dollars of one-shot agents are not visible |
| The orchestration resumes after a crash | Done (`resume`) |
| Real runs show it works with cheap models | Done: 66 runs, 9 Maestros, 6 baselines ([models](models.html)) |
| The harness can tell the team from one agent alone | Done (`--baseline`) |
| **The team beats one agent alone on some task** | **Answered in round 16** ([models](models.html)): it lifts a weak model (`gpt-oss-120b` from about 35% to 6 of 8, a vote over four runs does not) and does not beat a strong cheap one (DeepSeek alone: 8 of 8 even with ten traps). Development stops here: maintenance and the honest advice in the docs |
| Dangerous commands (`rm`, `git push`) approved by something other than the weak model | Not done. A box (`sandbox`) limits the damage; the commands are not filtered |
| Other agents (codex, goose, aider) as teammates in the challenge | Not done; no real run of those drivers |

## The three gaps left

1. **A task where one agent alone is often wrong.** Without it the layer's value is argued, not measured. Make a second scenario with a trap a single agent falls for (a rule hidden in a long file, a result that looks plausible and is not), run the baseline and the team on it, five runs each.
2. **More runs on the models that would be the default.** Three to six runs only separate a model that fails from one that works. Ten per model for Haiku 5.5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GPT-OSS 120B would settle the default team.
3. **Dangerous commands.** Either a policy file the person writes (which programs an agent may run) or the box as the default for every teammate with real keys. The second already exists as an option.

Nothing else blocks calling the layer finished. The first gap decides whether to keep investing in it.

# Checking a teammate's work

A cheap model is a poor judge of another model's answer. In our own runs a Maestro approved without looking, refused good work twice for no reason, sent the same message three times, and once asked the human a question instead of starting. So the judging is done by the program, not by the model.

## ask with a check

```bash
openmaestri ask "Dev" "Write flag.py that prints the flagged regions" --check "python3 flag.py" --retries 1 --then "Senior"
```

- `--check CMD` runs `CMD` in the teammate's folder (and in its container, if it runs in a box) with no API keys, no input and a time limit. Exit 0 means accepted. Only a Maestro can use it, because it runs a command on this machine.
- If the check fails, the failure goes back to the teammate by itself, in fixed wording, with the output cut to its first 20 and last 40 lines. The Maestro is not involved until the work passes or the corrections run out.
- `--retries N` is the number of corrections, 1 by default and never more than 2. A model that cannot fix it in two tries usually circles.
- `--then "Other"` hands the same task to another teammate when the first cannot pass.

The answer starts with one line the Maestro can act on without interpreting anything:

```
[gate] PASSED after 2 attempts
[gate] FAILED after 2 attempts: the check "python3 flag.py" exited with 1:
Traceback ...
```

## ask for a verdict

```bash
openmaestri ask "Auditor" "Judge this output against data/rules.md: Centro Leste Litoral Norte" --verdict
```

The reply must end in one line, and nothing else counts:

```
VERDICT: APPROVED - what was checked and found
VERDICT: REJECTED - Norte is listed but its revenue is under the limit
```

The older three-line block (`<<<VERDICT`, `STATUS: ...`, `REASON: ...`, `VERDICT>>>`) is still accepted. The single line is what weak models manage to write.

A loose "APPROVED", "NOT APPROVED", a missing reason or a placeholder such as `<reason>` is not a verdict. The program sends the reply back with the exact shape (as many times as `--retries` allows), and if it still does not fit, the answer is `[gate] FAILED ... no verdict line in the required shape`: the check fails closed. A valid `REJECTED` is a good answer, not a failure: `[gate] PASSED ... VERDICT: REJECTED: reason`.

## When a check failed and the Maestro answered anyway

If the Maestro answers the human while the last check on some teammate's work is a failure, the program adds a line to that chat message: `[openmaestri] Not verified: a check on the work of Dev: ... failed and was not fixed afterwards`. The human is not told "approved" about work that never passed, whatever the Maestro wrote. The report lists it as `unverified`.

## Loops

If the Maestro sends a teammate nearly the same message a third time within 15 minutes, the answer starts with a `[loop]` warning. The fifth is refused, with advice: say it differently with the exact error, or give the task to another teammate.

## One-shot agents

`agent` takes `--check` too. When the answer's work fails the check, the next driver of the fallback chain gets the task, the same way an exhausted account does:

```bash
openmaestri agent codex "Fix the failing test" --fallback opencode,kimi --check "npm test"
```

## Reminders to the Maestro

A weak Maestro often goes quiet after the human wrote: it asks a question the human already answered, says it "cannot run commands" without trying, or does the work itself. If the chat has no answer and its screen has not changed for 45 seconds, the program types a fixed reminder into its terminal, at most twice (`OPENMAESTRI_NO_NUDGE=1` turns it off). The report counts them.

## The report

```bash
openmaestri report          # or --json
```

One line per ask, check, verdict, correction, handoff and loop warning, in order, with the totals. It is written from what the program saw, so it does not depend on the Maestro remembering to tell you.

## Agents that wait for a human

Terminals that run an agent get `PAGER=cat`, `GIT_PAGER=cat`, `GIT_EDITOR=true`, `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive` unless you set them yourself. A model that runs `git log` or `git commit` without `-m` then fails at once instead of freezing the pane. A plain shell is left alone.

## Checking the checker

A reviewer's `verify.py` is only worth something if it can fail. The challenge checks that the Auditor's script prints the right list (an empty script or `sys.exit(0)` prints nothing) and that its output differs from the output of the script with the planted bug. If the oracle agrees with the bug, the run fails even when everything else looks green. Do the same in your own work: run the verifier once against something you know is wrong.

## Spending

```bash
OPENMAESTRI_BUDGET_USD=0.50 openmaestri      # when you start the daemon
openmaestri budget                           # read only, from any terminal
```

The program cannot see the API calls an agent makes, but a full-screen agent prints the session cost on its status line (OpenCode: `13.2K (10%) · $0.02`). openmaestri reads that number from each terminal, keeps the highest it has seen, and adds them up per workspace. At 80% of the limit you get a notification and a line in the report; at 100% every terminal of the workspace is stopped. Only the person sets the limit: there is no command for an agent to raise it. One-shot agents (`agent`, `run`) have no screen, so the dollars they spend are not counted. What the limit does for them: once it is reached, a one-shot agent that is running is stopped and a new one is refused (`agent`, `run`), so the cut has no back door. The stronger fence is a limit on the key itself at your provider (OpenRouter lets you put a credit limit on a key); use both.

## When the reviewer and the check disagree

A check is a fact (the command exited 0) and a verdict is an opinion. When a reviewer answers `REJECTED` right after the last check passed, the reply to the Maestro ends with a line saying so and asking it to run something that shows whether the reviewer's claim is true before it sends the Dev back to redo work that passed. The reviewer may still be right (a check can be incomplete), so nothing is overruled: the Maestro is only told, once, that the two disagree. The `report` lists it as a `conflict`.

## The state line

A Maestro that loses the thread (a weak model, a long session) has to rebuild from memory what was asked, checked and rejected. With `OPENMAESTRI_STATE_LINE=1` in the environment of the daemon, every `ask` ends with one line the program writes from its own events: per teammate the messages sent, the last check and the last verdict, then what is still open. It is facts only, no advice. It is off by default: in the one comparison made (`gpt-oss-120b` as Maestro, 7 of 8 right with the line and 5 of 8 without, see models.md) the difference is inside the noise.

## Where teammates run

```bash
openmaestri sandbox          # read only: in a box or on this machine, and which keys each one can read
OPENMAESTRI_DEFAULT_SANDBOX=my-agents:latest openmaestri    # every new teammate runs in this image
openmaestri recruit "Dev" --preset P --no-sandbox            # opt out for one
```

A teammate on this machine can read your files and the keys in your environment file and its account. `recruit` says so, by name and never by value: `Dev runs on this machine with access to your files and these keys: OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. The Maestro and a plain shell are never boxed by default. The default is the person's to set; an agent cannot change it. openmaestri does not see the commands an agent runs inside its own tool, so it cannot filter `rm -rf`; what it can do is keep the agent in a box where `rm -rf` only reaches that folder.

## Picking up after a restart

```bash
openmaestri resume
```

Every ask, check, verdict, correction, reminder and spending notice is saved with the workspace, so a restart or a crash does not erase it. `resume` prints the last events and what is still open (a check that failed and was not fixed afterwards). A Maestro started in a workspace that already has events gets the same text with its first message, so a replacement does not redo what already passed.

## What this does not do

It does not ask a second model to judge the first: two cheap models can agree on broken code. It does not accept a regex that is "close enough". And it does not hide the failure: when the corrections run out, the Maestro and the report both say so.
